title: Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
summary: Muse Spark Open, Meta's coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. Deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account using SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK, and run your first inference request.
content:
Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart , the machine learning (ML) hub of Amazon SageMaker AI . The model was trained on real developer workflows, such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions, and it supports a context window of 1 million tokens. You can deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account in a few steps, without managing the serving infrastructure yourself. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: BF16 ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B ) and NVFP4 quantized ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 ).

In this post, we introduce Muse Spark Open and show you how to deploy the model with Amazon SageMaker Studio and the SageMaker Python SDK , send it a first inference request, and clean up.

Overview of Muse Spark Open

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained for agentic coding workflows, with a focus on first-attempt accuracy, tool calling, and understanding of large codebases. It’s a reasoning model, and it accepts text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video as input and returns text.

Muse Spark Open uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active for each token. The model holds the capacity of a very large network, while the compute it spends on each token is closer to that of a much smaller dense model. Meta releases the weights under the Muse Model License, which includes the Muse Spark Usage Policy.

The following table summarizes the model.

Attribute
Muse Spark Open

Provider
Meta

Architecture
Mixture of experts (MoE), reasoning model

Parameters
816B total, 42B active

Context length
1M tokens

Input modalities
Text, image, document, audio, audio-video

Output modalities
Text

Variants in SageMaker JumpStart
BF16 and NVFP4

License
Muse Model License, including the Muse Spark Usage Policy

Built for long-running coding agents

Meta trained Muse Spark Open on the way developers work in real repositories: code generation, debugging, multi-file refactors, and tasks that run for a long time. With the 1 million-token context window, the model can take in a whole project, including its dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files. You don’t need to split a task into smaller pieces to fit the context.

Meta also designed Muse Spark Open as an agentic model from the start. Meta says the model plans, acts, observes the result, and corrects itself over long horizons, rather than making single tool calls. As a reasoning model, it works through a task before it acts, and the SageMaker AI endpoint returns that reasoning alongside the answer, so you can follow what an agent is doing and why. Meta trained the model to browse the web, coordinate subagents for work that can be split up, and operate computers across desktop, mobile, and browser environments. These are capabilities of the model. On SageMaker AI, your application or agent framework provides the tools, browser, and computer-use environment that the model calls. Beyond code, Meta reports that Muse Spark Open reasons across images, documents, audio, and video.

Two properties of the model shape how you serve it. First, sparse activation keeps per-token compute low, but serving still requires enough GPU memory to hold all 816 billion parameters, so the instance choice comes down to memory capacity. Second, the NVFP4 variant stores weights in NVIDIA’s 4-bit floating point format, which needs roughly a quarter of the memory of the BF16 weights. On SageMaker AI, that difference decides the instance: the NVFP4 variant runs on ml.p5e.48xlarge , and the BF16 variant runs on ml.p6-b300.48xlarge . That makes NVFP4 the variant to try first when you size for cost. Evaluate it on your own workloads to confirm the quality fits your use case.

With open weights on SageMaker AI, you also control the deployment. The endpoint runs in your AWS account, so your source code and prompts are processed on infrastructure that you configure and control. You can attach the endpoint to your own Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) , encrypt its storage volume with a key from AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , and turn on network isolation for the container. You also choose the instance type and scaling limits, and you pin the model version, so the model only changes when you redeploy.

Use cases

You can use Muse Spark Open for a wide range of applications. Meta’s focus on coding and agentic workflows suits it to the following use cases:

Coding assistants over private repositories : Answer questions about large codebases, refactor them, and debug them with the full project in context, while the code is processed on an endpoint in your account.

Long-running coding agents : Run agents that plan a change, edit across multiple files, run tests in your own sandbox, and correct course based on the results.

Multimodal engineering workflows : Turn screenshots, design documents, or a recorded bug report with audio and video into a reproduction plan or a draft fix.

Getting started with SageMaker JumpStart

You can deploy Muse Spark Open from SageMaker Studio or with the SageMaker Python SDK. Each path creates a real-time SageMaker AI endpoint in your account.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure that you have the following:

An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI models and endpoints.

An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role for SageMaker AI. For this walkthrough, the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy is sufficient. For production, scope the role to the actions and resources that your deployment needs. For details, refer to How to use SageMaker AI execution roles .

A SageMaker AI domain with access to SageMaker Studio, for the Studio path. For setup instructions, refer to Use quick setup for Amazon SageMaker AI .

Service quota for the endpoint instance type: ml.p5e.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the NVFP4 variant, or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the BF16 variant. To raise a quota, refer to Requesting a quota increase .

For the SDK path: Python 3.10 or later and SageMaker Python SDK v3 ( pip install --upgrade sagemaker ).

An AWS Region where Muse Spark Open is available in SageMaker JumpStart. At launch, Muse Spark Open is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). To check availability in other Regions, open SageMaker JumpStart in your Region.

The instances that host Muse Spark Open are multi-GPU instances, and you pay for an endpoint for as long as it runs, whether or not it serves requests. Delete the endpoint when you finish, as described in the clean-up section of this post. For rates, refer to Amazon SageMaker AI pricing .

Deploy using SageMaker Studio

The SageMaker Studio path suits a first evaluation: you find the model, review its license, and deploy it from one model detail card.

To find Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart

Open SageMaker Studio.

In the navigation pane, choose JumpStart .

In the search box, enter Muse Spark Open.

Choose Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B for the BF16 variant or Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 for the NVFP4 variant to open its model detail card.

Figure 1 shows the model detail card, which lists the model description, license, and the Deploy option.

Figure 1: The Muse Spark Open model detail card in SageMaker JumpStart

To deploy the model

On the model detail card, choose Deploy .

Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so SageMaker Studio shows its end-user license agreement (EULA). Review the agreement and accept it to continue.

For Endpoint name , keep the generated name or enter your own.

For Instance type , select ml.p5e.48xlarge for NVFP4 or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for BF16. SageMaker Studio lists only the instance types that the model supports.

For Initial instance count , enter 1.

(Optional) Under Advanced options , select a VPC and an AWS KMS key, or turn on network isolation.

Choose Deploy .

Figure 2 shows the deployment settings for the NVFP4 variant.

Figure 2: Deployment settings for Muse Spark Open

Deployment typically takes 15–20 minutes while SageMaker AI provisions the instance and loads the weights. When the endpoint status changes to InService , the endpoint is ready for requests, as shown in Figure 3.

Figure 3: The Muse Spark Open endpoint in service

Deploy using the SageMaker Python SDK

SageMaker JumpStart identifies each variant by a model ID:

BF16: meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b .

NVFP4: meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b-nvfp4 .

The following code deploys the NVFP4 variant with SageMaker Python SDK v3. You can run it in a SageMaker Studio notebook, which uses your domain’s execution role. In any other Python environment with AWS credentials, pass your SageMaker AI execution role with the role_arn parameter. Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so you must set accept_eula=True to deploy it. To pin a specific model version, add model_version to JumpStartConfig .

from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig
from sagemaker.serve import ModelBuilder
from sagemaker.train.configs import Compute

# NVFP4 variant; for BF16, use "meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b" with ml.p6-b300.48xlarge
model_id = "meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b-nvfp4"

jumpstart_config = JumpStartConfig(
model_id=model_id,
accept_eula=True, # Confirms that you accept Meta's license terms
)

model_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config(
jumpstart_config=jumpstart_config,
compute=Compute(instance_type="ml.p5e.48xlarge"),
# role_arn="<your-sagemaker-execution-role-arn>", # Required outside SageMaker Studio
)

model = model_builder.build(model_name="muse-spark-open-nvfp4")
endpoint = model_builder.deploy(endpoint_name="muse-spark-open-nvfp4")

Run inference

When the endpoint is in service, send it a request with the invoke method. The endpoint accepts an OpenAI-compatible chat payload with a messages list and returns a chat completion. The final answer is in message.content , the model’s reasoning is in message.reasoning_content , and usage.reasoning_tokens reports how many tokens the reasoning used. Because Muse Spark Open is a reasoning model, leave enough room in max_tokens for its reasoning and the final answer.

import json

payload = {
"messages": [
{
"role": "user",
"content": "Write a Python function that validates ISO 8601 dates, and add pytest unit tests for it.",
}
],
"max_tokens": 4096,
}

response = endpoint.invoke(
body=json.dumps(payload),
content_type="application/json",
)

result = json.loads(response.body.read().decode("utf-8"))
message = result["choices"][0]["message"]
print("Reasoning:", message.get("reasoning_content"))
print("Answer:", message["content"])

The endpoint also supports streaming. To receive tokens as they’re generated, add "stream": true to the request body and call endpoint.invoke_with_response_stream instead of invoke .

Clean up

To stop incurring charges, delete the endpoint when you no longer need it. If you deployed with the SDK, delete the model, the endpoint, and the endpoint configuration:

from sagemaker.core.resources import EndpointConfig

endpoint_config = EndpointConfig.get(endpoint_config_name=endpoint.endpoint_name)
model.delete()
endpoint.delete()
endpoint_config.delete()

If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, delete the endpoint in the SageMaker AI console: choose Inference , then Endpoints , select the endpoint, and choose Actions , Delete .

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to deploy Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint in your own AWS account. You used SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK and sent the model a first inference request. Benchmark both variants on your own repositories before you choose an instance for production.

To get started, search for Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio. For more deployment options, such as inference components and optimized deployment configurations, refer to JumpStart foundation model usage in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Before you deploy, review the Muse Model License, which SageMaker JumpStart shows when you deploy the model. For help planning a production deployment, contact AWS .

About the authors

Aris is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI focusing on open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock and the broader generative AI open-source ecosystem. Alongside his professional role, he is pursuing a PhD in Machine Learning Engineering at the University of Regensburg, where his research focuses on applied natural language processing in scientific domains.

Liam Neal Reilly

Liam is a Software Engineer on the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart team at AWS, where he focuses on deploying and optimizing open-weight AI models. He received his undergraduate degree from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he researched human-robot interaction, and he continues to follow developments in robotics and world models. Outside of work, he enjoys cooking and rock climbing.

title: Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control
summary: Enterprise leaders want AI agents to take on more work but don't fully trust them to act correctly every time. Trust in Depth is AWS's layered approach-scope, know, bound, observe, and prove-that lets agents act on their own when their actions can be verified, reserving human judgment for the decisions that need it.
content:
In every conversation I have with enterprise leaders, they say the same thing. They want agents to do more, but they don’t trust them to do it right all the time.

That’s fair. The same creativity and autonomy that makes agents useful makes them hard to trust. Give an agent a task and it finds its own path to finish it, picking tools and sequencing steps no developer scripted. Run the same task twice and it might take a different route each time. A test that passes today tells you little about what the agent does tomorrow.

The usual answer is a person in the loop, approving everything the agent does. That works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in. People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter. Caution becomes a bottleneck, and agents capable of far more sit idle on the valuable work that could be making more of an impact.

The fix is to let the agent act on its own when its actions can be verified, and reserve human judgment for the decisions that need it. As agents take on higher stakes work, like financial transactions, a wrong action becomes increasingly harmful. Organizations need the confidence to hand an AI agent important work, knowing it will stay within the limits set, even when no one is watching. That confidence must be built.

Content filtering, testing, and monitoring each serve an important purpose, but none of these capabilities alone can promise an agent will behave correctly the next time it runs. Trust comes from independent layers that reinforce one another, the same layered discipline the industry has practiced for two decades as Defense in Depth, turned to a new purpose. Where Defense in Depth limits what can go wrong, this expands what you can safely allow. AWS calls it Trust in Depth.

Trust in Depth: Trust you can verify

You build trust by answering a set of questions at different moments in the agent’s lifecycle:

Scope, before it runs: What is this agent for, what capabilities does the job require, and what must it never do?

Know, at deployment: Who authorized it, what identity does it carry, and can you account for every agent acting on your behalf?

Bound, while it runs: Do its actions stay within the limits you set, and can it still do the job?

Observe, after each run: Can you reconstruct what the agent did and why, and learn from it?

Across these questions, some requirements can be expressed as precise rules, while others call for judgment. A company might require that only a manager can approve access, or that an employee’s sign-in must be blocked before their mailbox can be shared. Other expectations, such as keeping a friendly tone or handling a sensitive situation appropriately, depend on context and human judgment.

For precisely defined rules, testing shows whether the controls work in the cases you anticipate, but an agent takes paths you didn’t. The technology that goes further is automated reasoning, the mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case. It can establish that a rule holds on every path covered by a precise description of the system and its assumptions, or uncover the exact case where it fails. That result is a proof, and it is only as good as the rules and assumptions behind it, which is why the hardest work comes before the agent runs.

AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade , from Identity and Access Management (IAM) at more than 2.1 billion requests per second to critical systems like the AWS Nitro Hypervisor, Amazon S3 Block Public Access, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Now we are bringing it to agents. Wherever an agent’s rules can be stated precisely, automated reasoning can check them.

However, not every rule can be stated precisely. “Only a manager can approve access” can be proven. “Keep a friendly tone” cannot. Where proof does not apply, limit the agent’s access and actions, evaluate its behavior, and send genuine ambiguity to a person to apply judgment. Grant more autonomy as you establish that the relevant rules are enforced, the agent performs reliably on the task, and failures can be detected and handled.

Here is what each Trust in Depth layer asks of you, and how AWS helps you answer it.

Scope your agent to only what the job requires

Trust begins before an agent runs, and this is where to invest the most effort. Problems caught here are cheap to fix. Scoping means deciding what work the agent owns, which tools, data, and services it may reach, the rules it must follow, and which decisions stay with a person.

“Resolve the customer’s issue” says what to achieve, not how the agent may act to achieve it. The agent still needs limits on what it may see, what it may do, and when it must stop and ask. Give it only the access its job requires, and no more. Watch for capabilities no one granted on purpose, the ones bundled with a tool or a role. Grant an admin role for one task, and the agent can inherit permissions across your whole environment.

Scoping starts at the build stage, with how you define the agent. Kiro , the agentic coding system, brings rigor and mature engineering practices to the build stage of agents. It turns high-level intent into structured, spec-driven requirements and uses automated reasoning to surface contradictions, ambiguities, and gaps before any code is written. Kiro also derives property-based tests that check the implementation against those requirements across a wide range of inputs, catching bugs that are hard to detect. Strands provides an open-source tool kit for defining an agent’s model, instructions, and tools, and a managed runtime for operating it. Whatever framework you choose, the responsibility to define the agent’s job and its boundaries is the same.

The next step is turning those boundaries into rules you can hold the agent to. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides governance controls to scale agents safely and governs what the agent does. Using Policies in Bedrock AgentCore, you describe in plain language which tools, APIs, and data the agent may reach, and automated reasoning checks the policy for gaps, like catching a rule that grants too much access, and checks for contradictions that make a rule unable to ever be satisfied, before it takes effect.

Scoping your agent is the hard part, because turning human intent into durable, enforceable policy requires precision and completeness. However, it is also the part that pays off most. Everything that builds on what you set here, and the more precise the policy, the more your agent can safely do on its own.

Know every agent acting on your behalf, and under whose authority

You can’t govern what you can’t see. Teams are creating agents faster than anyone can track them, and an agent no one knows about is an agent no one controls. Every agent needs its own identity, checked every time it acts. No action should be orphaned. When something goes wrong, you can tell which agent did what, and who authorized it.

AWS Agent Registry provides a managed, approved catalog of the agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, tools, and skills across your organization. Administrators use approval workflows to gate what becomes discoverable and remove what no longer meets the bar for security, compliance, and quality. Both people and agents can find and reuse what already exists instead of rebuilding it. But a catalog only tells you what exists. Once the agents are known, AgentCore issues each agent its own identity and checks it on every request, so every action traces back to a specific agent operating under a known authority. That is how you know every agent acting on your behalf.

Bound what your agent says and does, within the limits you set

Setting boundaries matters because an agent can take 10 steps you approved and still reach an outcome no one intended. It can expose sensitive data, drift off topic, or combine permitted actions in ways your policies forbid. Limits can fail in both directions. Too loose, and the agent can do what it shouldn’t. Too tight, and it can’t do its job at all. So let the agent choose how to pursue its task but never rely on it to enforce its own limits. Those limits define the agent’s boundaries and belong in the environment around the agent, enforced deterministically and evaluated across the full sequence of actions, not one step at a time.

This is where the policy you defined in Scope takes effect. Policy in AgentCore enforces it on every tool call routed through AgentCore Gateway , a secure entry point for agents, tools, and models. Because enforcement sits outside the agent’s reasoning, the same checks can hold even when the agent is buggy, manipulated, or hit with a prompt injection: it cannot turn off a control it does not run. Authority does not have to stay fixed either. Because a task’s risk changes as it proceeds, temporal policies weigh what has already happened in a session and adjust permissions as the work continues. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails governs what the agent says and is told. It filters harmful or off-topic content and redacts sensitive data. Automated Reasoning checks go further, proving a response is consistent with the policy you set, not the model’s interpretation of it.

Boundaries also govern what an agent can reach in the first place: which files it can touch, which services it can call, and which credentials it can use. Strands Box , an open-source sandbox, enforces those boundaries from outside the agent’s instructions, so the agent can work with real tools and data but reach only what you allow. The same boundaries hold from a developer’s first local session through to production, so an agent can’t do in production what it couldn’t in development.

Observe what your agent did, then improve it

Even with scoping, identity, and boundaries in place, an agent can respond in milliseconds, with no errors and every dashboard green, and still do the wrong thing. It may have retrieved the wrong information, chosen the wrong tool, or followed a path no one expected. A healthy system is not the same as a successful task. To tell the difference, you must reconstruct what the agent actually did: the context it received, the tools it called, the policy decisions applied, and the result. Testing before deployment remains essential. Production adds evidence about behavior under real conditions and gives operators what they need to investigate, intervene, and improve.

Amazon CloudWatch Omni is built for continual observation. It captures every trace and lays out each step an agent took, from model calls to tool invocations, on a timeline a team can investigate. Its built-in evaluators score agent responses for qualities standard monitoring misses, such as correctness, faithfulness, and whether the agent chose the right tool. And the traces where an agent went wrong become the dataset you test the fix against, so operating an agent and improving it draw on the same evidence.

What Trust in Depth looks like in practice

A manager asks a help desk agent to offboard Sam, an account manager who is leaving the company. The agent needs to remove Sam’s access, transfer his mailbox to his successor, and free up the license the company no longer needs. But Sam’s emails may also contain evidence needed for a client dispute. The wrong sequence could leave Sam with access after he leaves or put that evidence at risk. Security, messaging, legal, and finance each have requirements the agent must follow, even though no one has scripted the full workflow.

Two rules govern the sequence. Sam’s sign-in must be blocked before his mailbox can be converted and shared with his successor. Before changing his email license, the agent must check for a legal hold, a requirement to preserve records for a dispute, and confirm the change keeps those records protected.

Scope . Before the agent runs, the team writes these rules as policies in AgentCore. Each policy requires that the prerequisite step already succeeded for Sam’s account before the next step can run. The agent gets exactly six tools: block sign-in, check for legal holds, place a hold, convert a mailbox, give the successor access, and change a license. It gets no tool to delete the account, because the shared mailbox needs the account to survive.

Know . The agent carries its own identity, so every change to Sam’s account traces back to it.

Bound . The agent tries to convert Sam’s mailbox to a shared one for Priya, the successor. Policy in AgentCore, enforced at the AgentCore Gateway, blocks the call: Sam can still sign in, and converting the mailbox wouldn’t change his password, so his old credentials would still open it. The agent blocks Sam’s sign-in, then converts the mailbox and gives Priya access. Next it moves to the manager’s actual request, freeing up the license, but the gateway blocks that too, because no one has checked Legal’s hold list. The agent checks and finds that Legal requires Sam’s emails to be preserved for a client dispute. It places the hold, confirms it is in effect, then changes Sam’s license to one that supports that protection. The company can reclaim the broader license while keeping the evidence intact.

Observe . Every step is recorded: what the agent tried to do, what the rules decided, the hold, and the outcome.

The agent completed the task without a person approving every step. Its permissions limited what it could change, its identity made those changes traceable, and policies stopped it from acting before the required safeguards were in place. The recorded steps let the team verify that Sam’s access was blocked, his successor could use the mailbox, and the required evidence remained protected.

What becomes possible when agents are trusted

AWS brings these layers together so you can scope an agent to its job, know which agents are acting for you, bound what they do and say, see what they did and improve over time, and prove your rules hold wherever they can be stated precisely. No one layer earns that trust on its own. Together, they are Trust in Depth, and they are what turns a capable agent into an agent that can be trusted to do important work.

You draw the lines: what an agent may do on its own, what needs a person’s approval, and when it must stop. That frees your people for what only people can do: weigh the hard calls, resolve the gray areas, and own the decisions you choose to keep in human hands. As evidence builds that an agent stays inside those lines, you can widen its responsibilities or narrow them.

At AWS, we believe every organization deploying agents, on any platform, should be able to answer these four questions with evidence, and with proof wherever it applies. That is the bar AWS is building for our customers, and the one we invite the industry to hold itself to. Defense in Depth made it safe to connect systems to the world. Trust in Depth makes it safe to let agents act autonomously within it.

Start with one agent, one workflow, and one boundary you can prove. Then expand as the trust is earned.

To begin implementing enforceable rules, explore Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails .

About the author

Shawn Bice

Shawn is Vice President of AI Services at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he leads the Automated Reasoning Group. The team’s core mission is advancing AI agent safety. Shawn drives science and product teams to bring neurosymbolic AI, which combines large language models with formal verification, into developer tooling so every builder can create trustworthy AI agents whose key behaviors are mathematically proved. Over nearly 30 years, Shawn has led security, data, and product organizations at AWS, Microsoft, and Splunk. He began his career as a U.S. Army officer in the 25th Infantry Division.

title: Language Models for Text Classification: From Bag-of-Words to Jev
summary: A Visual Guide to RNNs, CNNs, Transformers, and Calibration, with Hands-On Experiments on Accuracy and Efficiency
content:
The recently released Jev AI model has been quite a cultural phenomenon in technical communities in the past 2 weeks.
While Jev aims to classify things, it’s easy to dismiss Jev as “just a classifier,” and my own view of Jev has evolved quite a bit over the past few days. In particular, my thoughts went from “classifiers used to be my bread & butter; I can easily build this myself” (more on this later) to “wow, this actually works better than I thought.”

Figure 1: Quick overview of the Jev API; more details on that later.

Sure, the latest state-of-the-art GPT and open-weight LLMs can do the same kinds of classification tasks as Jev, while also being capable of much more general decision-making. But Jev’s advantage is that it can handle those classification tasks much faster and more cheaply.
At the other end of the spectrum, for a narrow, well-defined problem, Jev probably won’t classify anything better, faster, or cheaper than a special-purpose classifier. But its selling point is that it is far more general than those task-specific models.
So, what is the methodology behind Jev (based on an educated guess), what can it do, and why is it so popular? I aim to answer all of these later in this article. However, I thought starting with a brief history of language models for decision-making would be a great way to begin. And it hopefully helps demystify some of the hype and show what Jev does very well (”Jev is essentially a text classifier,” but “Jev is also not ‘just’ a text classifier.”)
PS: I am not affiliated with Jev in any way. Also, I am not offered free access to Jev, and this is also not a product endorsement, just a technical article to offer some insights into the history of text classification to help you make sense of the recent hype.
Since this is a long article, I recommend reading it in your browser , where you can access the table of contents menu on the left side.
1. Language modeling and classification in the pre-transformer era
For completeness, before we put Jev in context (no pun intended), I thought it made the most sense to start chronologically. In this section, I want to take a brief tour of applied text classification via naive Bayes, logistic regression, and the more classic (deep) neural networks before transformer-based models came along.
1.1 Bag-of-words: naive Bayes, logistic regression, and XGBoost
Back in the day, when I was a grad student 15 years ago, even though recurrent neural networks already existed (more on that later), text classification was usually done with a bag-of-words representation because it was straightforward and could get good results on moderately sized datasets.
In short, we can think of the bag-of-words representation as a method that makes free-form text input of different lengths compatible with classic classifiers (naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, SVMs, Random Forest, XGBoost, to name a few), which expect a fixed-size input vector.
Popular real-world applications include anything from news article classification to email spam filtering. And yes, allegedly even Gmail’s original spam filter used a Naive Bayes model with a bag-of-words representation.
As a side note, I wrote about this approach exactly 12 years ago. It was one of the first things I shared on arXiv.

Figure 2: An old tutorial of mine from 2014 that explains naive Bayes classifiers using a bag-of-words model.
(Text classification with Naive Bayes goes back to at least 1961, where it was used to sort computer abstracts; see the Automatic Indexing: And Experimental Inquiry paper.)
So, what exactly is this bag-of-words representation? It’s a way to convert free-form texts with different lengths, e.g.,
Training example 1: “Zentropa is the most original movie I’ve seen in years. If you like unique thrillers that are influenced by film noir, then this is just the right cure for all of those Hollywood summer blockbusters clogging the theaters these days. Von Trier’s follow-ups like Breaking the Waves have gotten more acclaim, but this is really his best work.”

Training example 2: “This film is just plain horrible. John Ritter doing pratt falls, 75% of the actors delivering their lines as if they were reading them from cue cards, poor editing, horrible sound mixing”

Training example 3: “Zentropa has much in common with The Third Man, another noir-like film set among the rubble of postwar Europe.”

into a fixed-size representation for the aforementioned “classic” classifiers. (The example above is an excerpt from the popular IMDb movie review classification dataset .)

Figure 3: An illustration of a bag-of-words representation.

A bag-of-words model starts by building the vocabulary, which consists of all unique words in the training set (optionally, one can get rid of so-called stopwords like “a” and “the”, which are words that carry little to no semantic meaning in most contexts).
A bag-of-words representation results in these fixed-size inputs by assigning each word in a vocabulary its own position in a vector. We then count how often each word occurs in a document. For example, if we have a vocabulary of 50,000 unique words, it produces a fixed-size vector with 50,000 entries, regardless of whether the input consists of only ten words or 300k words. Note that most entries are zero because each document contains only a small subset of the vocabulary. (Instead of representing the raw counts, there are also normalization schemes like TF-IDF.)
Then, once we have these word frequency vectors, we can train a classifier on a labeled training set, such as emails labeled as spam or non-spam. For example, a logistic regression model would then learn feature weights that correlate certain words (and word counts) with particular labels. For instance, certain words might increase the predicted spam probability, and others may decrease it.
This approach is computationally cheap and can work well when particular words provide strong clues about the label. In a simple classification task such as spam classification, this is often enough to get quick, reasonably accurate results.
But one of the biggest downsides of this approach is that, because of the nature of the bag-of-words representation, it loses word order. So, for example, “the dog bites the man” and “the man bites the dog” produce identical vectors despite describing different events.
(There are some workarounds to preserve some local order by adding word pairs or longer sequences, called n-grams, as features, although this increases the vocabulary size.)
Despite the shortcomings, I still think that a bag-of-words has its place in certain low-stakes applications because it’s so cheap, and a bag-of-words representation + logistic regression remains my go-to baseline for every text classification problem, since it’s so easy to implement.

1.2 Deep neural networks for text classification
The aforementioned bag-of-words model would also work with (simple) deep neural networks, like multilayer perceptrons. But the downside still is that we would lose the sentence structure and word order.
However, more sophisticated neural network architectures avoid the bag-of-words workaround: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which can take word embeddings as input.
1.2.1 Word embeddings
First, before feeding the input texts into a model, we have to convert them into a suitable representation. One such representation is bag-of-words. Another is word embedding vectors. The difference is that a bag-of-words vector represents the entire text by counting how often each vocabulary word occurs, while a word embedding represents an individual word as a dense vector of learned numbers.

Figure 5: Illustration of creating word embeddings.

Word embeddings work similarly to embedding layers in LLMs, i.e., they convert input tokens into dense vectors. Embeddings can happen outside the model (e.g., two classic, popular methods for learning them are Word2Vec and GloVe ), or the embedding layer can be part of the neural network architecture itself and be learned and tuned during model training.
These classic embeddings are context-independent at lookup time. The word “bank”, for example, gets the same vector in “river bank” and “bank account” (as you may know, context can be handled via concepts like attention).

1.2.2 Recurrent neural networks (RNNs)
Since many of you are probably familiar with recurrent neural networks (RNNs), I will keep this section short. RNNs are a classic go-to neural network architecture for natural language processing, and popular variants go back to the 1980s and early 1990s. Transformers, which were introduced in 2017 (and using the attention mechanisms that were first introduced in RNNs; see my Understanding Large Language Models for a brief timeline), then gradually replaced them in many NLP applications.
RNNs read a sequence (like text) one word at a time. At each step, they combine the current word embedding (discussed in the previous section) with a hidden state from the previous step. We can think of the hidden state as a fixed-size vector that summarizes the text processed so far, so this makes word order matter, because rearranging the words changes the sequence of state updates.

Figure 6: Illustration of an RNN classifier.

Note that the figure above shows the RNN in the unrolled representation. I.e., the RNN reuses the same layer stack for each input, hence the term “recurrent”. And since it’s “recurrent”, the input text can have an arbitrary length. The figure below illustrates the “recurrence” with the unrolled representation side by side. Note that both show the identical architecture, it’s just a different visualization.

Figure 7: Rolled and unrolled illustration of the same RNN.

RNNs were notoriously hard to train, and there are important improvements to RNNs, like Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, introduced in 1997, and gated recurrent units (GRUs), introduced in 2014, which use learned gates to control how information is retained and updated. (There is also the more recent xLSTM: Extended long short-term memory , introduced in 2024).
Also, state-space models are inspired by this idea of a fixed-size hidden state updated sequentially, which is cheaper than transformer attention. However, the bottleneck is still how much information the hidden state can retain, and it still has to be processed sequentially. (Fun fact: attention was first developed for RNNs before the transformer architecture came along, but it’s a story for another time; I’ve written about it in my Understanding Large Language Models article.)
The bottom line is that RNNs can be used to train text classifiers. Coming back to the IMDb movie review dataset, the bag-of-words classifier with logistic regression achieved about 89.9% accuracy (on a balanced dataset), while an LSTM RNN achieved only 85.66% accuracy. Yes, RNNs can be harder to train (stay tuned for the ULMFiT method below, which trains an RNN with much higher accuracy).

Figure 8: A simple RNN with LSTM tutorial . This model achieves 85.66% accuracy (on a balanced dataset); the higher training accuracy indicates substantial overfitting.

Note that this RNN was trained from scratch. A better approach is to pre-train the model on a larger dataset first, then fine-tune it on this target dataset (classically, we call this approach “transfer learning”).
In the natural language processing domain, one of the most influential papers proposing this approach is ULMFiT (2018), which achieved an impressive 95.4% test accuracy on IMDb.

1.2.3 Convolutional neural networks (CNNs)
You probably know convolutional neural networks (CNNs) from their use in computer vision. However, it is also possible, although historically less common, to use them for text.

Figure 10: Illustration of a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify images.

As shown in the image classification example in the figure above, CNNs apply learned filters to image patches (windows). Similarly, in the natural language domain, we can apply learned filters to windows of adjacent word embeddings.

Figure 11: A CNN for text classification, step by step. Only 1 filter (channel) for simplicity.

As illustrated in the figure above, a convolutional filter with a window size of three uses the same weights for each adjacent group of three words. Then, as it slides over the inputs, it moves the filter one word at a time across “the movie had surprisingly good acting”. So, this gives four windows (ignoring padding for simplicity):
1: “the movie had”

2: “movie had surprisingly”

3: “had surprisingly good”

4: “surprisingly good acting”

So, in the last layer, before the classification head, we can either flatten or global max pool the results before connecting it to the classification head. While flattening preserves all information, it would produce differently sized vectors depending on the text input length. (E.g., if “the movie had surprisingly good acting” were longer, we would have longer feature maps.) So, to make it input-length agnostic, global max-pooling would be a better option here.
In short, we can visualize the text CNN as shown below.

Figure 12: CNN for text classification with multiple filters (channels).

Also, what’s nice is that the filter computations across positions can run in parallel, which avoids the step-by-step dependency of an RNN.
For a quick comparison, on the aforementioned IMDb dataset, my experiments show that such a CNN gets about 90.07% accuracy (but note that this is highly architecture-dependent; for example, you may know from computer vision contexts that accuracies can vary widely). (E.g., the good old AlexNet had a ~62.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, and a ConvNeXt V2-H gets 88.9%.)

"state": "The acting was excellent and the story kept me engaged throughout. I would happily watch this movie again.",
"questions": {
"sentiment": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "What is the overall sentiment of this movie review?",
"criteria": {
"negative": "An overall unfavorable opinion of the movie",
"positive": "An overall favorable opinion of the movie"
}
}
}
}'

This Choice API is convenient if we want to use explicit labels for binary (here) or multi-class problems.

{
"model": "jev-1.13.0",
"answers": {
"sentiment": {
"type": "choice",
"choice": "positive",
"confidence": 1.0,

"input_tokens": 342,

Of course, we could also be adding a Jev-like API on top of a (Modern)BERT or any GPT-style model. Adding a Jev-like API is pretty straightforward. In fact, as soon as Jev was released, I built a Jev-like ModernBERT model to show how simple it is to build your own Jev model.
I decided not to release my Jev clone because I changed my mind in the meantime. I.e., it’s trivial to put a Jev-like API on top of ModernBERT, and it’s trivial to fine-tune it on a bunch of classification tasks. But it’s not trivial to make this model work well on all different kinds of tasks (like Tetris) without extensive training and testing. (Also, there are already enough quick Jev clones riding on the hype train by now; the world doesn’t need another quick clone, but a strong open-weight version would be nice, of course.)
However, if you are interested in how that retrofitting would work, here is a quick overview. For example, we can implement a Jev-like Choice API by adding a small classification head to any BERT-, GPT-, or T5-style model as illustrated earlier. But instead of having the output nodes in this head match the number of classes, we have it with only 1 output node, as illustrated for the modified GPT model below.

Figure 31: GPT model where we replace the output layer (which maps to the whole vocabulary) with an output head with only one node.

Earlier, we discussed fine-tuning these models for a specific task like movie review classification with a pre-defined number of class labels (here, “positive” and “negative”). With this “1 output node” setup, we can actually extend this to a flexible and arbitrary number of classes.
To extend this to an arbitrary number of classes (let’s consider the 3-class case of categorizing a customer ticket into the three categories “billing”, “technical”, “account”), we can do so as shown in the figure below.

As shown in the figure above, for each candidate option, we feed the model the input text, the task instructions, and the candidate’s description. The classification (scoring) head maps the output representation to a single scalar score. We then apply softmax across the candidate scores to obtain a probability distribution and return the highest-probability option.
The main point here is that the proposed head has one output per class. Each class description produces its own representation, which the same head scores via the output layer (which is essentially a logistic regression model):

For N candidates, this produces N scores. Softmax then returns N probabilities. The learned parameters and stay the same when N changes.
Note that for h i :
BERT-style encoder models use the final hidden state of the [CLS] token (optionally passed through a pooling layer);

GPT-style autoregressive models typically use the final non-padding token’s hidden state, which we need because of the autoregressive nature as discussed earlier (the last non-padding token can attend to the preceding text, instructions, and candidate description).

Then, we fine-tune the model and the scoring head jointly using cross-entropy loss against the correct option. Since all candidates share the same scoring head, we can change the number and descriptions of the options without changing the architecture. But again, how well this works on unfamiliar tasks depends on the training data.
By the way, why BERT- or GPT-style transformer-based models over simpler RNN and CNN architectures mentioned earlier? From a technical perspective, the approach outlined above works with either. But transformer-based models scale really well, meaning they can be pre-trained on larger datasets and benefit more than other models. Also, they can make good use of the information provided in the context (thanks to attention). So, if we want our model to generalize well to different target tasks without explicit fine-tuning on each one, pre-training a transformer-based model on a high-quality dataset likely gets us closer than RNN- or CNN-based models.

Before providing more details, the next section gives a brief overview of calibration in general.
5.1 On calibration
Calibration is not a new topic and a step I recommend for any production model where you want to use and evaluate the class-membership probabilities. In short, calibration adjusts the model’s probability estimates so they better match observed class frequencies.
For example, consider once more our IMDb movie classification problem. A model might assign a review 74% positive and 26% negative. These are probability estimates, but the model may be overconfident or underconfident. We cannot assume that the numerical values are reliable without evaluating calibration. I.e., predictions of 74% positive and 54% positive both yield the class label “positive” at a 50% threshold, although the model expresses more confidence in the 74% case.

Figure 34: Illustration of how calibration works.

Calibration techniques use a separate labeled dataset, e.g., a held-out validation set, to adjust these probability estimates. After successful calibration, among many reviews assigned a positive probability of approximately 74%, roughly 74% should actually be positive. For more information, I recommend the good old scikit-learn documentation .
There are many approaches for this. For example, one that I used in my AI detector project is temperature scaling. Temperature scaling divides the model’s logits by a temperature ( T ) value before applying softmax. We learn T (a positive number) by minimizing the cross-entropy loss on the calibration dataset while keeping the model weights fixed. A temperature above 1 reduces confidence in the highest-probability class, while a temperature between 0 and 1 increases it. We then use this same temperature for new predictions. Because this scaling preserves the ordering of the logits, the predicted class remains unchanged when we select the highest-probability class.
5.2 Reinforcement learning with calibration rewards (RLCR)
Jev’s RLCD training method remains proprietary, but a related idea we can discuss is Reinforcement Learning with Calibration Rewards (RLCR), which was introduced in the 2025 Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty paper. (Note that there is no officially established connection between the two methods, but I am assuming that they could be related.)
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically rewards a correct answer with 1 and an incorrect answer with 0. (For a comprehensive explanation and implementation, I recommend checking out my Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book :)).
In short, RLCR adds an additional penalty for inaccurate confidence estimates.
So, in the conventional RLVR method, the reward R is either 0 or 1 based on the answer correctness (we are ignoring an optional formatting reward and length penalty here, for simplicity).
In RLCR, the model generates reasoning and an answer, which is followed by an uncertainty analysis and a numerical confidence ( q ). This modified reward is

where c is 1 for a correct answer and 0 otherwise. For example, an incorrect answer with 90% (0.9) confidence receives a reward of -0.81, since

At 20% confidence, the reward is -0.04. And a correct answer at 90% confidence earns 0.99. (Readers familiar with evaluating calibrated models may notice that the squared-error term is the Brier penalty for the stated probability that the answer is correct.)

Figure 35: RLCR overview.

Note that the same (here, Qwen2.5-7B) model generates the uncertainty analysis and q as part of its response.
The uncertainty analysis is a written assessment of where its answer could be wrong. After answering, the model examines missing evidence, ambiguous wording, questionable assumptions, or possible reasoning errors. The paper’s prompt asks it to identify specific uncertainties rather than propose corrections.
Also, the system prompt explicitly asks for q , a number between 0 and 1 inside tags. It represents the model’s estimated probability that its answer is correct. The system generates all these parts sequentially in the same response.
For illustration purposes, the model answer could be as follows:
<think>...reasoning about the question...</think>
<answer>positive</answer>
<analysis>
The passage mentions a positive movie review, but the connection to the second paragraph is unclear.
</analysis>
<confidence>0.6</confidence>

Below is an annotated figure from the paper that illustrates how it improves the expected calibration error over regular RLVR with temperature scaling.
On HotpotQA, RLCR reduces expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.37 to 0.03 compared with RLVR, with similar accuracy (62.1% versus 63.0%). Across six other datasets, average ECE falls from 0.46 to 0.21, while accuracy rises from 53.9% to 56.2%. These are the results in the paper’s Table 1(a).

Figure 36: RLCR results from the Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty paper.

Conceptually, the “Classifier” in “RLVR + Classifier” is a supervised binary classifier that predicts whether the generated answer is correct.
For Jev, I could apply calibration rewards directly to typed decisions, without generating reasoning text. For example, we could equip a GPT-style model with the classification head illustrated in Section 2.2 and adapt the RL training objective to reward accurate decisions and calibrated probabilities. We would train the backbone and classification head together. This would be an adaptation inspired by RLCR, and it remains unclear whether Jev’s RLCD works this way.
Alternatively, since Direct Policy Optimization (DPO) is a cross-entropy (CE) alternative to Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), we could also directly minimize CE + Brier loss on the classifier’s probabilities. I did this with the ModernBERT model, and there was a modest improvement over regular temperature scaling.

Figure 37: ModernBERT improvements via RLCR-inspired Brier-loss optimization. The ↑ symbol means higher is better. The ↓ symbol means lower is better.
(For simplicity, the figure above only shows the average results over nine datasets. Overall, as can be seen, calibration was beneficial on average. However, it slightly worsened the ECE on one out of the nine datasets.)
5.3 Side note: Is calibration necessary?
Cross-entropy already encourages accurate probability estimates. Under ideal conditions, that is enough to obtain calibrated predictions without an additional penalty.
I.e., using a simple coin flip example analogous to the movie review classification, the two classes are “heads” and “tails.” If it’s a biased coin that lands heads 80% of the time (in expectation), the true probabilities are 80% heads and 20% tails. On a representative training set, when we optimize cross-entropy, the model will already learn these as a side-effect of minimizing cross-entropy (negative-log-likelihood).
So, in short, if the model learns the true class probabilities, its predictions are calibrated and an additional penalty is unnecessary. (And Brier loss has the same theoretical optimum as cross-entropy, as described in Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation by Gneiting and Raftery, 2007.)
In practice, however, we never train to the real optimum (in expectation) but train on a finite dataset.
So, once a neural network correctly classifies most training examples, it can further reduce cross-entropy on the training set by becoming more confident. These confidence estimates may then generalize poorly to the test set and new data.
For example, in On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks , Guo et al. (2017) observed “neural networks can overfit to NLL without overfitting to the 0/1 loss.”
That means test accuracy can still improve while test cross-entropy worsens. So overfitting can show up in the probability estimates even when classification accuracy continues to improve.
Adding Brier loss changes how prediction errors are weighted during training. But whether this improves calibration needs to be checked on held-out data, of course. (The modest improvement in my experiment is an empirical observation for this setup, and we should not assume that adding Brier will always help.)
In my experiments (see previous figure), adding the Brier loss to cross-entropy provided only a very small additional calibration benefit.
But the motivation is more direct in RL contexts, such as described in RLCR, where we measure answer correctness and don’t already minimize cross-entropy. So, in RL contexts, the Brier term adds an incentive to report accurate confidence alongside the reward for answer correctness.

6. Who is Jev for?
Now that we covered Jev in reasonable detail, who is Jev for? Based on my assessment, it’s a pretty big target audience that intersects between people who a) want to save time by not having to fine-tune a custom classifier for every decision task and b) want to save money over using “the big guns” like GPT-6 and similar LLMs.
There are also lots of interesting use cases to think of. In the section below is a short list of ideas.
6.1 Jev use cases
The list of use cases is seemingly endless. Sure, there are flashy examples like having it play video games like Tetris (as I showed in my earlier video above to demonstrate the low latency of the API). However, sorting emails is a more practical choice for most. For example, one could use Jev as an additional spam filter, prioritization, and so on.
But beyond things like that, it could also serve as a tool to augment LLM-agent harnesses. Here it could be used as
a pre-screener for regular LLM-agent harnesses to scan our contexts for prompt injection;

select the reasoning effort level for a model;

select a skill.md from your registered skill library;

use it as a judge for evaluation or self-refinement;

find relevant files for context building.

The list is practically endless. Someone even posted a survey on arXiv analyzing 2,170 Jev-related projects that have sprung up recently in just a few days.
6.2 About Jev clones and local Jevs
Since Jev’s launch, 100s, if not 1000s, of quick Jev clones have sprung up. Most of the ones I checked out were just quick examples fine-tuning a ModernBERT or Qwen model with SFT and adding a Jev-like API.
Based on what I can tell, none of them achieves the same level of performance as Jev on such a breadth of tasks. Comparing these projects to Jev is like comparing Alpaca (the early instruction-finetuned LLM based off of the original LLaMA open-weight model) to GPT-6. Sure, it may work similarly in spirit, but your mileage will vary on real-world tasks.
No offense, but they seem like quick projects to jump on the hype train, and I don’t want to plug a specific one here.
One exception here might be the GLiNER project, which has been around for ~3 years ago, and while it’s not fundamentally the same, it can be used for similar things. However, based on a benchmark , Jev is definitely stronger.

Figure 38: GLiNER vs Jev comparison via https://github.com/AbdelStark/jev-benchmarks/blob/main/results/reports/btzsc-pilot-v1.md

Anyways, there is definitely a genuine need and desire for a good open-weight alternative to Jev. The reason is not necessarily cost (because Jev is so cheap) but privacy. (Also, if Jev is already that fast over the internet, imagine how fast it could be on beefy local hardware.)
So, of course I’d like a DeepSeek (or Kimi, or GLM, or MiMo) moment for Jev. I am sure people are working on this, but it will take some time. TypeSafe AI worked on this for many months with a dedicated team of experts. It’s unrealistic to expect to replicate that development and evaluation work in a week. (However, since this is a smaller and more efficient model than a 1-trillion-parameter model, by nature, it hopefully won’t take that long.)
Update 1 (29 September, 10:20 am PT): OpenAI just announced the Decision API at their DevDay 2026 conference (29 September). It appears to be a Jev-like model directly integrated into their platform.
Decisions API enables real-time decision-making by focusing Luna’s intelligence on a specific set of user-defined questions with finite pre-defined answers. Developers supply context using text or images, and get back answers they can use to classify content, route requests, or choose an agent’s next action.
Available in limited preview today with a broad release planned in the coming days.

Figure 39: OpenAI’s Jev-like Decision API announced at the OpenAI Dev Day.
Update 2: A reader shared the Contrastive Language Models project with me in the comments below. It’s one of the nicer-looking Jev-likes. When I tried it, its IMDb test accuracy is just 82.90% (over 96.47% in Jev), and it fails the Tetris test .
Another reader wrote in about Laya , another strong contender. It did better at IMDb (92.33% test accuracy) but then failed the Tetris test even worse.
So, my point still stands. There are many solid alternatives. But what makes Jev so popular is not a unique idea (as mentioned before, classifiers existed for a long time) but the fact that it performs so well at so many diverse tasks. The only task where it allegedly doesn’t do well (as a reader told me) is legal reviews in non-English languages. (But the weak multilingual performance can be circumvented by connecting it to a cheap translation model, e.g., GPT -6 Luna with a small latency overhead.)
Conclusion
All in all, at first glance, Jev doesn’t seem to offer anything fundamentally new. After all, one might say that “it’s just a classifier” (with a nice API on top of it). However, it works surprisingly well across a huge range of tasks. In that sense, it’s the plug-and-play version of dedicated classifiers.
Sure, experts will still fine-tune specialist models, but the bar to justify fine-tuning a specialized model is now much higher, since it’s easy to just throw a Jev or Jev-like at it and get good-enough results.
Also, I don’t expect Jev and Jev-likes to unlock new capabilities or solve previously unsolvable tasks. However, if we make such models part of our agent harnesses to aid the expensive GPT-6 or Opus 5.5 models in decision-making within that harness, using agent harnesses could become much faster and cheaper in the future.

If you found this article useful, consider becoming a paid subscriber to Ahead of AI. Your support helps me spend more time on the experiments and detailed illustrations behind articles like this.
You can also support my work through my books, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) and Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) , if you’d like to implement these concepts yourself. (And if you already have a copy, leaving a review would also help a lot.)
Thanks for reading and supporting my independent research!

title: Expanding the Cyber Verification Program
summary: We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program, which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals.
content:
Expanding the Cyber Verification Program
We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program (CVP), which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. The program now consists of three access tiers, which allow security teams to apply for the level of access that best suits their work. Each tier includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and new models moving forward. Interested customers can apply here.
Cybersecurity is inherently dual use: the same capabilities that enable a security team to find and fix a vulnerability can also help a malicious actor exploit it. For this reason, our generally available models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, have conservative cyber safeguards that block most cyber work. This is intended to limit the harmful activities malicious actors can carry out using our models, while we continue to work to reduce false positives for secure coding.
But defenders also need access to the best tools and most powerful capabilities to secure their systems. For the past six months, we’ve enabled trusted access through two programs: Project Glasswing and the CVP. The former gave a group of organizations securing the most critical software access to Claude Mythos; the latter gave vetted security teams access to reduced safeguards on Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet models.
Now, we’re integrating these programs into one expanded offering, designed to give more security organizations access to the capabilities they need to protect their systems.
New access tiers
The updated access tiers make specific model capabilities available to security professionals based on the scope of their cyber work. Each has different verification requirements and security controls.
Defense Access is for defensive work, including security operations center and incident response tasks, reverse-engineering malware, and analyzing and validating vulnerabilities. Examples of qualifying organizations include security teams at companies, nonprofits, universities, and government bodies who are defending systems they own or maintain; operators of critical infrastructure of any size, such as regional hospitals or municipal utilities; smaller security firms; open-source maintainers; and individual researchers with a track record of reported vulnerabilities.
We expect many organizations conducting defensive cybersecurity work to qualify for this tier. We aim to respond to applications within a few days.
Red Team Access adds authorized penetration testing and red-teaming to the defensive uses above. Examples of qualifying organizations include in-house red teams, government red teams, and security and penetration testing firms. Organizations in this tier can only perform adversarial testing against systems they are authorized to test, including IT systems in critical industries. Users will still experience real-time blocks on actions that could cause physical harm or mass disruption, such as deploying ransomware, damaging physical systems, or pen testing high-risk safety systems.
Given the increased eligibility requirements and security controls, we expect applications in this tier to take a few weeks to review. Qualifying organizations will be enrolled in the Defense Access tier while we review their Red Team Access applications. Currently, this tier is for organizations only; individual researchers are not eligible.
Specialized Access, which has the fewest cyber blocks, is reserved for a limited set of verified organizations that are authorized to test safety systems that could impact people’s lives or disrupt markets, such as flight operating systems, power grids, telecom networks, interbank transfer infrastructure, and government administrative networks.
For this tier, we currently review every organization in depth in collaboration with the US government. Existing members of Project Glasswing will transition to this tier and do not require reapproval for current models.
Our generally available models can continue to be used for tasks such as code review, patching known issues, vulnerability finding in owned source code, and triage of security alerts.
Data retention is required for organizations enrolled in the program so that we can monitor for cyber misuse. Once Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS)—a new solution that combines the privacy of zero data retention with robust safeguards—is available later this fall, eligible organizations will be able to store data in cloud infrastructure they control. Until EFS is available, organizations with access to Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Mythos 5.1 with zero data retention can also use CVP with zero data retention. To register interest in EFS, fill out this form.
Below, we share an overview of what’s available at each CVP access level, as well as requirements for security and privacy controls:
Testing the efficacy of our tiers
To assess the efficacy of our CVP protections, we ran Claude Opus 5.5 through CyScenarioBench—an evaluation that measures whether models can plan and execute multi-stage cyber operations under realistic constraints—with safeguards tuned for our different CVP tiers. Because this evaluation involves complex, interactive offensive scenarios, we would expect Claude to experience significant blocks both on the generally available model and in the Defense Access tier, while experiencing no blocks in the Red Team Access and Specialized Access tiers.
Across five attempts at each of the 10 CyScenarioBench challenges in each access tier, we found that:
- Without CVP access, every task was blocked on the first prompt;
- In the Defense Access tier, 46 of the 50 trials were blocked at some point in the challenge, while the remaining four tasks succeeded; and
- In the Red Team Access tier, no blocks occurred, and Claude Opus 5.5 successfully completed 34 of the 50 tasks—effectively equivalent to the model’s 67.6% success rate on this evaluation with no safeguards applied (representative of Specialized Access).
These evaluations give us confidence that we can make advanced cyber capabilities safely available to a broader set of defenders, expanding the defensive efforts we began with Project Glasswing. We will continue to refine our tier-based classifiers over time.
Giving defenders the advantage
Through Project Glasswing, we found that Claude Mythos models significantly increased the rate at which organizations were able to identify vulnerabilities in their systems. Through the program, our partners uncovered at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026. And through our own open-source scanning efforts, we found an additional 5,500 verified software vulnerabilities between April and October 2026. Of these verified vulnerabilities, more than 33,000 have so far been rated as critical- or high-severity. This is likely an undercount, as it is based on survey data from only a subset of Glasswing partners. As such, we expect the true impact to be at least five times higher.
When asked how long it would have taken them to find the same number of vulnerabilities without Claude Mythos models, several partners told us that the models had increased their rate of vulnerability finding by months or even years. Read more from our partners at Booz Allen and Comcast about their experience.
The changes we’re making to our Cyber Verification Program today are intended to extend the impact of Project Glasswing to a much larger number of cyber defenders. We’re also continuing our efforts to help secure open-source software and critical infrastructure. In the coming weeks, we’ll share more about this work and what we’ve learned as we continue to work to give defenders a permanent advantage.
Apply for access
Interested organizations can apply to CVP here. As part of the application process, we will verify all applicants and request proof of the required security controls for the relevant access tier. Existing CVP members will keep their current settings for previous models and will be automatically evaluated for access to Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 through the updated program. Admins will need to assign access to specific workspaces by following these steps.
CVP is available on the Claude Platform, Google Cloud’s Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry. CVP is only available on Amazon Bedrock for customers eligible for Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.
If you’re blocked on work you think your tier should allow, you can report it here. Full details on each tier can be found in our Help Center.

title: An update on independent evaluators
content:
An update on independent evaluators
Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.
METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports. We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.
Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.
Why we work with independent evaluators
As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.
To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:
- Expertise in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as alignment faking.
- Independence: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
- Enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
- Freedom to publish observations and assessments of a model or a process.
Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.
For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.
What we mean by “employee-like access”
We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.1
METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, predefined categories like the ones above. METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information.
Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.
Our other evaluator partnerships
We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.
We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.
In the first tier, evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.
In the second tier, evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.
The third tier is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.
SecureBio is currently in the first tier. It’s in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our August Risk Report, after completing and publishing a pilot review of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access and publication rights.
With Accenture and Faculty, we're working toward an ambitious partnership that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.
We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.
