title: Sizing Lakebase Search: lessons from a real app and 4 million passages
summary: Slide Hub is an internal Databricks app. Field engineers use it to find and reuse...
content:
Slide Hub is an internal Databricks app. Field engineers use it to find and reuse slides from about 700 internal presentations: event talks, product decks, and architecture decks. A search bar finds single slides by meaning and by keyword, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server gives AI agents the same search. The app stores its slides, votes, search telemetry, and change history in Lakebase Postgres. We use Slide Hub as the baseline to benchmark Lakebase Postgres. It is a real app with a real use case and real users, so its numbers show how the database behaves under an actual workload.
This post is for developers and architects who build apps on Databricks and want search inside the app's own Lakebase Postgres database. It assumes that you know SQL and the basics of PostgreSQL. If you plan a search bar or an agent tool on Lakebase Postgres, the numbers below help you choose the compute size before you go to production.
This post shows how Slide Hub runs search inside Lakebase Postgres, what limits it under load, what it costs, and how Lakebase Search behaves from 1M to 4M rows of a public corpus.
Lakebase Search became generally available in September. It is a set of Postgres extensions, so it runs next to the application tables. The app does not copy data to a separate search system. The developer does not maintain a second transaction path.
Two CREATE EXTENSION statements enable the components. lakebase_vector stores embeddings, vectors of numbers that represent the meaning of a text, and supports the lakebase_ann index for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. lakebase_text supports the lakebase_bm25 index for BM25, a standard method that ranks text by the query words it contains. lakebase_tokenizer is optional. The ANN index uses IVF partitioning, which groups similar vectors so a query reads only a few groups, and RaBitQ quantization, which compresses each vector to about 1 bit per dimension. BM25 scores text with the <@> operator.
Slide Hub’s 23k slide rows sit in the same serverless Lakebase Postgres instance as the votes, telemetry, change history, previews, and both indexes. The app reads the data and the indexes inside one connection and one permission model.
Slide Hub runs hybrid search. It combines vector search, which finds slides with a similar meaning to the query, and BM25 keyword search, which finds slides that contain the query words. Each method returns a short list of its best matches, the candidates. One SQL statement carries the whole ranking policy. It ranks each candidate list, fuses the two rankings, applies the app filters, and joins the votes. Search and app logic share one connection, one set of grants, and one commit.
Slide Hub takes 200 candidates from each method. It fuses the two lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) at k=60: a slide scores 1/(60 + its rank) in each list, and the two scores add. A similarity gate of 0.70 rejects vector matches that are too far from the query to be useful for this embedding model. Title tiers add weight when the query matches a slide title. Notes receive weight 0.5. Scope filters restrict the result to assets the user has permission to see.
A search request uses two separate computes, and either one can set the limit.
Lakebase Postgres compute runs the database. Lakebase Postgres sizes it in Compute Units (CU). One CU allocates about 2 GB of RAM to the database, with its share of CPU and local SSD. A compute autoscales between a minimum and a maximum size from 0.5 CU to 64 CU, and the maximum can be at most 16 CU above the minimum. Fixed-size computes go up to 112 CU, and computes up to 32 CU can scale to zero.Postgres stores tables and indexes in 8 KB pages. Lakebase Postgres keeps recently read pages in a Local File Cache (LFC) on the compute. The cache grows with the CU size and can use up to 75% of the compute's memory. A page that is not in the cache comes from storage, which takes longer.
Databricks Apps compute runs the Slide Hub web server. Its size is fixed per app. A MEDIUM app has up to 2 vCPU and 6 GB of memory, and a LARGE app has up to 4 vCPU and 12 GB. Slide Hub runs one app instance. Each Python worker process in it holds a pool of 8 database connections, so 2 workers open at most 16 connections and 4 workers open at most 32.
For each request, the app embeds the query text, sends one SQL statement to Lakebase Postgrse, and returns the result. To find the limit, the test changes one side at a time. It pins Lakebase Postgres at one CU size and changes the app, or it keeps the app and changes the CU size. A load generator simulates users that send search requests, and it raises the number of users in steps. The list shows requests per second and the median latency (p50) at 500 users for each Lakebase Postgres size and app size.
Up to 4 CU, Lakebase is the limit. A LARGE app with twice the workers and connections adds nothing at 1 CU. At 1 CU the search statement averaged 146 ms and read 14.9M pages from storage, with a file cache of 1.5 GB. At 8 CU it averaged 34 ms, with a cache of 12 GB, and throughput rose about 50%.
From 8 CU, the app is the limit. 16 CU with the same MEDIUM app adds only 4%, and its database connections sit mostly idle. A LARGE app with 4 workers at 16 CU reaches at least 662 req/s, and there the load generator was the limit. Size the query first. Then scale Lakebase Postgres until the app workers are the limit, and then scale the app.
Takeaway: Find the limit before you scale. Below 8 CU, add Lakebase Postgres CU. From 8 CU, give the app more workers.
The connection pool is still necessary. At 50 users the app reached 45 req/s and 2.4 s p95 without the pool, and 85 req/s and 0.7 s p95 with it. The embedding cache made no measurable difference under load.
The candidate limit sets the number of pages a query touches. On a cold cache, that number sets the latency. Slide Hub shipped with 1,000 candidates per method. The docs pattern uses 40. The candidate-limit experiment changed only candidate_limit and measured 20 public queries in three states. Cold is the first query after the compute scaled to zero, with an empty cache. First-touch is the first run of a query on an awake compute. Repeat is the same query run again, with its pages in the cache. Pages touched counts the pages a query reads from any source. Top-10 overlap is the share of the top 10 results that match the result at 1,000 candidates.
At 200 candidates, 90.5% of the top 10 stays the same, and the reported number of matches is 81% of the number at 1,000 candidates. Users rarely page past 200 results, so Slide Hub now ships 200. Measured end to end from a job in the same cloud region as the app, a cold search at 200 candidates took 2.9 s, and a repeat search took 40 ms. The cold time has two parts. The connection waits about 1 s while the endpoint wakes up. Then each query reads its pages from storage until the cache warms. The first query on a new connection also pays about 75 ms of planning.
Takeaway: Keep the candidate pool small. 200 candidates keep 90.5% of the top 10 results, read about a third of the pages of 1,000 candidates, and halve the cold latency.
The scale tests use MIRACL English, a passage corpus built from Wikipedia. The full corpus has 32,893,221 passages. We embedded it with gte-large-en-v1.5, a 1024-dimension open model, the same size as the Slide Hub embeddings. We self-hosted the model on one A10G GPU at 379 passages per second. The whole corpus took 2.95 GPU-hours, against $48.87 for the same work on a model-serving endpoint. The GPU vectors matched the endpoint vectors (mean cosine 1.0000, minimum 0.9978).
We built three subsets: 1M, 2M, and 4M passages. The lakebase_ann index grew with the corpus: 5.8 GB at 1M, 11.5 GB at 2M, 23.0 GB at 4M. A binary COPY loaded all 4M rows in 19 minutes at 8 CU.
Lakebase Postgres holds about 1.6 GB of file cache per CU. Scale raises one question: what happens when the index is larger than the cache? Each test cell is one corpus size at one CU size, so the cache is a known fraction of the index. We call that fraction the cache ratio: cache size divided by vector index size. A ratio of 1.0 means the index just fits. The hit rate is the share of the pages a query reads that do not come from storage.
We ran three query mixes against each cell. The uniform mix sends a new title every time and never repeats, the worst case for a cache. The skewed mix draws from a pool of 20,000 titles with a Zipf distribution, a common model for search traffic. The cold mix runs the first queries right after a wake-up, when the cache is empty. Before the uniform and skewed measurements, a warm-up runs the same mix until the hit rate stops changing. We call the results after the warm-up warm.
The hit rate depends on the cache ratio. The corpus size does not change it: the 2M and 4M points fall on one curve. At a ratio of 0.07 the skewed mix hit 45% of its pages in cache. At 0.57 it hit 86%. At 1.14, where the index just fits, it hit 97%. The uniform mix sits a few points lower, because it reuses nothing.
That gives a sizing rule. Measure your index size, pick a CU size for the cache ratio you want, and read the hit rate off the curve. The ratio works across corpus sizes, so a test at 2M predicts the behavior at 4M.
Takeaway: Size the cache from the vector index, not from the row count. A cache about as large as the index serves 95% to 98% of the pages without storage.
Warm vector p50 fell from 187 ms at a ratio of 0.07 to 4 ms at a ratio of 2.3. Hybrid search stayed near 800 ms until the ratio approached 1, then dropped to 33 ms. The keyword half of the hybrid query reads the most pages, so it gains the most from a full cache.
Takeaway: Vector search takes 160 to 230 ms while the cache holds less than a third of the index, and 11 to 23 ms once the whole index fits.
A miss is one 8 KB Postgres page that is not in the Local File Cache. In the vector index, one page holds one or two embeddings. One page read from storage costs a fixed amount of time. Across every measured query, execution time grows by about 252 microseconds per missed page for vector search and 316 for hybrid. A query that misses 2,000 pages pays about half a second. A full cache removes almost all the misses. This is why the cache ratio sets the latency: it sets how many pages each query reads from storage.
Takeaway: Each page from storage adds about 0.3 ms. Multiply the storage misses per query by 0.3 ms to estimate what the cache saves you.
Hold the cache ratio near 1.0 and change the corpus size. Warm vector latency stayed between 11 and 23 ms from 1M to 4M. Warm hybrid latency stayed near 276 ms. The cold queries, which read from storage, grew with the corpus: a cold vector query went from 44 ms at 1M to 133 ms at 4M, and a cold hybrid query reached 911 ms at 4M.
This is the honest form of “you do not need the whole index in memory”: you do not, because the architecture keeps compute memory flat. RaBitQ stores about 1 bit per dimension, 32 times smaller than float32, and IVF reads only a few partitions per query. The index is storage-backed, so compute can be small or scale to zero. The queries that miss the cache pay for the miss, and the cache ratio controls how often that happens.
Takeaway: Grow the compute with the corpus, and warm latency stays flat. Only the queries that miss the cache get slower as the corpus grows.
The throughput test sent hybrid queries straight to Lakebase Postgres, without the app, so it measures the database alone. It opened 1, 4, 16, or 64 connections to Lakebase Postgres at the same time. Each connection sent a query, waited for the answer, and then sent the next one. The chart shows the total number of queries per second across all connections. When a line goes flat, more connections do not finish more queries. Lakebase Postgres is then at its limit, and each query waits longer instead. The load generator's own CPU stayed near zero, so Lakebase Postgres set every number.
On the 4M corpus the skewed mix reached about 4 queries per second at 2 CU, 15 at 8 CU, and 65 at 16 CU. At 64 connections, the median wait for one query was 14.5 s at 2 CU, 5.2 s at 8 CU, and 343 ms at 16 CU. The uniform mix at 16 CU peaked at 30 queries per second, because it never reuses a page. Throughput scales with the compute size and the cache ratio together.
Read these as the cost of cache misses under load. Most queries in a real app repeat or cluster, so the warm hit rate, not the uniform mix, sets steady-state capacity.
Takeaway: More CU buys throughput twice, with more CPU and a larger cache. Going from 8 CU to 16 CU raised the skewed throughput from 15 to 65 queries per second.
The lakebase_ann index is approximate. Recall@10 is the share of the true 10 nearest passages, from an exact search over all vectors, that the index also returns. The index splits the vectors into partitions (IVF), and lakebase_ann.probes sets how many partitions a query reads. Recall@10 barely moved with the corpus size at the default probe count: 0.74 at 1M, 0.75 at 2M, and 0.75 at 4M. More probes trade latency for recall.
With the default index at 4M, the default 109 probes gave a recall@10 of 0.74 in 3 ms, and 2,000 probes gave 0.95 in 49 ms. An index built with build_mode = 'quality' raised recall at every probe count: 0.80 at the default probes in 3 ms, and 0.97 at 2,000 probes in about the same time as the default build. Its build took 52 minutes at 16 CU. Raising lakebase_ann.epsilon to 4, the highest value it accepted in our tests, added less than 0.3 points.[9] Recall depends on the data and the embedding model, so measure it on your own data and pick the probe count your app needs. Lakebase Search supports a single index of over 1 billion vectors.[1]
Takeaway: Build the vector index with build_mode = 'quality'. At the default probes it raised recall@10 from 0.74 to 0.80 in about 3 ms, and at 500 probes it reached 0.91 in 13 ms, which takes 1,000 probes and 20 ms on the default build. The cost is the build time: 52 minutes for 4M passages at 16 CU. Raise the probes only if your app needs more recall.
Lakebase cost follows use. A suspended compute incurs no compute cost, and storage is billed separately. Lakebase was about 1% of the Slide Hub 30-day bill. Slide Hub is an internal app, and a slower first search after 5 idle minutes is acceptable for its users, so its production database scales to zero when nobody searches.
The scale evaluation was cheap. The self-hosted embedding of the whole corpus took 2.95 GPU-hours, against $48.87 for the model-serving endpoint. One in-region load ramp ran for 14 minutes and cost $0.13 at list price: $0.11 for the app and $0.02 for Lakebase Postgres, which autoscaled between 0.5 and 1 CU and used 0.21 CU-hours. Up to 1,000 users the ramp served 109,602 requests without errors. The cells ran at 0.5 to 16 CU and suspended between runs. In our workspace's billing tables, one CU-hour is 0.213 DBU: about $0.085 at the Premium list price and $0.11 at the Enterprise list price in AWS US East.
Takeaway: Lakebase Postgres bills compute only while it runs. The 14-minute load test used $0.02 of Lakebase Postgres compute, and that compute cost was about 1% of the Slide Hub 30-day bill. For production, set the minimum to 0.5 CU instead of scaling to zero. At list price that costs about $31 to $40 a month, and searches no longer wait about 1 s for the compute to wake or start with an empty cache.[11] Let dev and test branches scale to zero.
MIRACL English is open. The corpus is Apache-2.0, and its passages come from Wikipedia under CC BY-SA. The embedding model gte-large-en-v1.5 is Apache-2.0.This post reports aggregate metrics only. The same test runs with any 1024-dimension model: swap the embedding step, keep the table, the indexes, and the search.
Think of Lakebase Postgres as a reader at a desk in front of a large bookshelf.
Databricks has three searches, and each one fits a different job. Pick the one that sits next to your data.
Slide Hub runs all of this in one Lakebase Postgres database: the app data, the vector index, and the keyword index. Start with the Lakebase Search docs, then run the same test against your own data.

content:
Predictive AI Functions give business users and SQL analysts high-quality forecasting, anomaly detection, driver analysis, and prediction — without advanced ML expertise.
by Jonathan Brito and Gary Shambat
Data teams all get asked the same questions: "what will sales be next quarter?," "why did this metric move?," and "is this recent data outside the norm of what we typically see?" Answering these advanced analytics questions usually means handing the work to a data science team to build models and manage infrastructure. This creates a bottleneck where business users wait in line and many questions never even get asked.
Predictive AI Functions, now in Beta, remove that bottleneck by letting analysts and business users run advanced analytics like forecasting, driver analysis, and anomaly detection, all through built-in functions backed by state-of-the-art ML models. These SQL-native functions can be called directly in SQL, invoked in Genie with plain-language questions, or embedded in dashboards. Because Databricks maintains the models centrally, teams get high-quality, consistent answers without building or managing infrastructure.
This launch adds four new SQL native functions and improved accuracy to ai_forecast:
ai_forecast: project a time series into the futureai_top_drivers: find which segments most drove a change in a metricai_detect_anomalies: flag outlier rows in temporal dataai_predict_value: predict continuous values (regression)ai_predict_class: predict categorical values (classification)
To showcase how these functions can be used across Databricks, we'll walk through examples in dashboards, SQL, and Genie using the NYC taxi trips dataset.
Dashboards are where teams watch the metrics that run their business, and often where they turn to see where those metrics are headed next. With ai_forecast, teams can project metrics and surface those forecasts alongside the rest of their reporting.
The new ai_forecast makes it easy to get high-quality forecasts without any tuning. It's powered by a transformer-based time series foundation model, pretrained on a huge, diverse collection of time series the way a large language model is trained on text. Because it already recognizes common patterns like seasonality and trends, it produces accurate forecasts on your data with no tuning required.
The visualization below uses ai_forecast to project the monthly ride volumes in the NYC taxi trips dataset through the end of 2027. The forecast reveals expected seasonal patterns in taxi demand, providing a data-driven view of where ridership is headed.
The new ai_forecast not only handles general patterns automatically, it also introduces features to let teams add factors specific to their business. With built-in holiday support, teams can automatically account for local events like Christmas dips and school-holiday spikes. Teams can also specify external covariates, feeding in the factors that drive a metric, such as pricing changes or marketing spend, so forecasts better reflect their business.
This launch also introduces four new functions for the ad-hoc advanced analytics questions commonly asked by data teams.
Each one, like ai_forecast, is a native SQL function. Analysts can call them directly in the SQL editor or a notebook, run them across hundreds of millions of rows, and feed the results into their queries and pipelines alongside the rest of their work. Compared to developing custom models for similar functionality, this compresses development time and increases accessibility to more users.
For example, the query below aggregates NYC taxi trips into a daily revenue time series and passes it to ai_detect_anomalies, which automatically fits a model to the data and flags unusual days.
These same functions will be available to business users through Genie (ai_top_drivers is available today, with ai_forecast, ai_detect_anomalies, ai_predict_value, and ai_predict_class coming soon). Anyone can ask a question in plain language, like why revenue dropped last quarter or which customers are likely to churn, and Genie calls the right function to return a grounded, model-backed answer, with no SQL or ML expertise required.
The query below uses ai_top_drivers to automatically identify which time-of-day and weekday/weekend segments contributed the most to the change in NYC taxi fare revenue between January and February 2016. It ranks each segment by its absolute and relative revenue impact, revealing that weekday midday hours drove the largest gain while the weekday evening rush was the biggest drag.
Because these functions use tailored machine learning methods, they enable Genie to answer questions a general-purpose LLM cannot reliably handle on its own.
These functions all deliver high-quality predictions backed by production-grade ML models. Because Databricks maintains those models centrally, that quality stays consistent across every surface, so teams get the same trustworthy result whether a prediction runs in a dashboard, in SQL, or through Genie.
Forecasting shows this most concretely. We used fev-bench to benchmark the new ai_forecast against functions from a leading cloud data warehouse. Task win rate is defined as the percentage of tasks (measured by scaled quantile loss) where one system achieves a lower probabilistic error than the other. Here's how the options compare:
ai_forecast outperforms other cloud data warehouse providers as well as the previous version of ai_forecast. With Predictive AI Functions, teams get industry-leading accuracy out of the box, on every surface, with no tuning required.
Predictive AI Functions turn questions that once required a data science team, like what's next, why did it change, what's wrong, and what's the value, into answers business teams can get themselves, right where they already work: in dashboards, in Genie, and in SQL. The result is advanced analytics for everyone: high-quality predictions that are easy to use, with no models to build or infrastructure to manage.

content:
Code scanning AI Scan for pull requests is now generally available. It complements CodeQL by finding vulnerabilities in pull request changes for languages and frameworks that CodeQL does not currently cover, including PHP, Shell/Bash, Terraform configuration (HCL), Dockerfiles, JSP for Java, Blazor for C#, and more.

How it works

AI Scan runs automatically on pull requests when code scanning and the repository’s effective AI Scan setting are enabled. Findings appear alongside CodeQL results on the Conversation and Files changed tabs, with an “AI” indicator to distinguish them from CodeQL alerts. Findings can include an explanation of the security risk and a suggested autofix.

AI Scan findings are advisory. They do not fail the code scanning check and cannot block pull request merges through ruleset requirements. AI Scan does not run on pull requests from forks or pull requests created by Dependabot.

Availability

AI Scan is available for public repositories owned by organizations or personal accounts. For private and internal organization-owned repositories, GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security is required. A GitHub Copilot license is not required.

Billing

AI Scan for pull requests consumes Code Security AI Credits. AI Credit usage is displayed in the “AI usage” section of enterprise billing and licensing as the “Advanced Security” product. You can also set SKU-level budgets for Code Security AI Credits. Learn more about usage-based billing .

Learn more about AI Scan for pull requests and billing for GitHub Advanced Security AI features .

title: Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts general availability
summary: Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts is now generally available. It remediates alerts by working across your codebase the way a developer would: it explores relevant files, proposes a fix,… The post Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts general availability appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
content:
Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts is now generally available. It remediates alerts by working across your codebase the way a developer would: it explores relevant files, proposes a fix, and reruns CodeQL to confirm the fix closes the alert before opening a pull request for your review. Agentic autofix is available to GitHub Code Security and GitHub Advanced Security customers on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

How it works

When you assign a code scanning alert to Copilot, it:

Explores relevant files across your codebase.

Generates a proposed fix.

Validates the fix works by rerunning CodeQL.

Iterates if needed, then opens a draft pull request ready for your review.

The pull request includes a summary of the fix, why it closes the alert, and the validation steps Copilot took to confirm that it works. When the pull request containing the fix is ready, you can instruct Copilot to make further changes to it by commenting on the pull request or interacting with the session in the Agents tab of your repository.

How to use it

When enabled, agentic autofix replaces the free Generate Fix option on individual code scanning alerts with an Assign to Copilot button.

You can use agentic autofix:

From any code scanning alert on the repository’s default branch, by assigning the alert to Copilot.

In the list of security alerts in your repository or security campaign, by selecting up to 25 alerts for Copilot to fix together in a single pull request.

Via the Update a Code Scanning Alert REST API by setting assignees to ["copilot-swe-agent[bot]"] .

Agentic autofix supports code scanning alerts on the repository’s default branch. Alerts detected only on pull requests or other branches cannot be assigned to Copilot.

Access

Agentic autofix requires an enterprise administrator to enable access to it via the new “Agentic autofix” policy in Advanced Security policies.

Once the policy is enabled by an enterprise administrator, an organization or repository administrator can turn on agentic autofix in the Code Security settings for the organization or the repository.

Access also requires a Copilot billing method to be defined.

Billing

Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts consumes AI Credits from your Code Security budget and GitHub Actions minutes. AI Credit usage will be displayed in the “AI usage” section of enterprise billing and licensing as the “Advanced Security” product. You can also set SKU level budgets for Code Security AI credits. title: Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
summary: Accelerating the search for novel antimicrobial peptides using Google Antigravity for Science.
content:
Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
New antibiotics are urgently needed to help with rising levels of antimicrobial resistance, but searching for new therapeutics is often a slow, labor-intensive process. With Google Antigravity, our agentic development platform, this process can now be made easier.
Google Antigravity provides an agentic science workbench that empowers biologists to discover, structurally evaluate, and prioritize promising targets quickly, compressing what used to be a fragmented search over multiple databases into a single session. It also helps researchers scan through millions of previously uncharacterized proteins in the UniProt database using ProtNLM, a model that predicts biological function from amino acid sequences.
This technical walkthrough shows how biologists used Google Antigravity to uncover a novel antimicrobial peptide candidate which has predicted activity against the pathogens involved in respiratory tract infections. The lead identified here is now undergoing wet-lab validation.
Finding new antimicrobial peptides
Rising antimicrobial resistance is one of the most pressing global health crises of our time and could result in an estimated 10 million annual deaths globally by 2050. To prevent this, we urgently need to discover novel therapeutics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly bacteriocins, offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics because they have naturally evolved to target fundamental vulnerabilities in competing bacteria, from cell envelopes to essential intracellular machinery, making it difficult for pathogens to develop resistance.
The exponential growth of genomic and metagenomic sequencing has populated global databases with billions of natural amino acid sequences. This pool of natural data has already produced globally used bacteriocins like Nisin, alongside recent genome-mined breakthroughs such as Darobactin, Dynobactin, and Lariocidin.
Many, however, remain locked within the unannotated "dark matter" of protein databases, with their function uncharacterized because they arenât similar to known proteins. For example, the world's leading public resource of protein sequence and functional information, UniProt, holds millions of sequences with unknown functionality, transferred directly from genome sequencing projects.
To bridge this gap, Google developed ProtNLM (Protein Natural Language Model), a deep learning model trained to directly read the underlying evolutionary âgrammarâ of amino acid sequences. This allows the model to predict biological function directly from raw protein sequences, enriching millions of previously unnamed UniProt entries with high-confidence functional labels.
Collaborative intelligence
Scientific discovery is rarely a single step process; finding viable candidate proteins requires human intuition and iteration to incorporate new empirical evidence. Working in Antigravity, the researcher and AI agent begin by setting a focused biological goal: find and computationally validate novel AMPs in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae. During an interactive, multi-turn session the researcher steers the scientific strategy, deciding which questions to ask and what evidence to collect, while the agent handles the heavy lifting of cross-database orchestration, structural analysis, and literature synthesis.
The candidate we uncover in this walkthrough represents a biologically plausible lead backed by structural and genomic evidence but it still requires wet lab validation. What makes this meaningful is how dramatically it lowers the barrier to everyday biological workflows, turning days of fragmented database triage into a single collaborative session. While this session focused on a narrow amino acid window in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae, researchers can take the conversation in any direction, such as layering in new filtering criteria, exploring different sequence lengths, or targeting other priority pathogens. By broadening the search from human commensals to environmental microbes and beyond, scientists can guide the agent across UniProt to discover novel AMP candidates at scale.
A shared 3D canvas for interactive collaboration
A protein's 3D structure can help us understand its biological function. Examining a candidateâs predicted fold in space is key. To provide this end-to-end workflow in a single workspace, we are introducing the Biomolecular Structure Viewer, a 3D visualization tool embedded directly into Antigravity.
The researcher and agent work together over a shared visual state. As the agent retrieves structures from AlphaFold Database or the scientistâs own predictions, it can dynamically drive the viewer. For instance, it can highlight key functional regions to visually explain its hypotheses. Crucially, this awareness flows both ways: actions like highlighting specific residues or pinning notes directly onto a binding pocket are synchronised back to the agent. A researcher can simply mark a region of interest in 3D space and ask, for example, "How might this Î²-strand affect Lipid II binding?", allowing the agent to immediately reason over the exact structural context the scientist is looking at.
Accelerating Scientific Discovery
Historically, uncovering insights like those in the workflow demonstrated above required fragmented and specialised software: writing custom scripts to query databases, manually exporting files to 3D modelling programs, managing disconnected genomic tools and working with multiple experts to design the wet lab assays. Because wet-lab validation remains resource-intensive, narrowing the search space to only the highest-confidence leads upfront is critical. Using Google Antigravity allows researchers to navigate the vast biological search space efficiently while leveraging accurate protein function predictions from a domain-specific model.
Google Antigravity executes this end-to-end scientific reasoning in one place. This allows scientists to spend more time evaluating high-quality hypotheses, running experiments in the lab and solving research challenges.

title: Google DeepMind and Singapore Government collaborate to build fine-tuned AI model for scam detection
summary: Learn how Google DeepMind and GovTech Singapore uses lightweight on-device Gemma models to intercept conversational scams in private chats with zero cloud data egress.
content:
Google DeepMind and Singapore Government collaborate to build fine-tuned AI model for scam detection
Collaborating with the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) to protect users without compromising privacy.
Scams, such as investment fraud, fake job offers, and impersonation of public officials make up over half of Singaporeâs reported crimes, and account for more than S$4 billion in losses since 2019. At the same time, scam tactics have shifted from simple phishing to complex social engineering, whereby attackers manipulate victims with convincing conversations before requesting money. Such scams now account for up to 80% of all losses.
To address this, Google DeepMind and the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have been working together as part of our National AI Partnership with the Singapore Government. Together, we've fine-tuned a privacy-preserving, on-device scam detection model.
On-device AI protection without compromising privacy
Generic models often struggle with local deception techniques, making scam detection harder. To address this, Googleâs lightweight Gemma model was fine-tuned on local scam conversations. These ranged from impersonations of public institutions, banks, and local figures, to trending regional schemes. This ensures the fine-tuned model will be able to distinguish benign social chatter from genuine manipulation when deployed in applications installed by citizens.
Unlike traditional threat detection, which relies on server-side scanning of messages in the cloud, this model can process conversation data directly on-device. When integrated into applications, this will allow faster analysis of conversation patterns to detect manipulative intent and help citizens act before financial or credential exposure can occur.
The roll out of the model within applications will be carefully phased and developed in partnership with the Singapore Government. When deployed, the model will only be able to access on-device conversations with the user's consent, in accordance with the terms of use of that application. As the model runs entirely on-device, neither the Singapore Government nor Google, will be able to access usersâ conversations through its deployment.
Under the hood: local context and edge efficiency
When the model detects manipulative conversational patterns, it triggers a real-time warning directly on the user's device advising them to pause and exercise caution before sharing sensitive information or funds.
Running a complex scam classifier model on modern smartphones is no easy task, with battery efficiency being a critical area of concern. To do this, we're relying on a two-stage pipeline:
- Stage 1: A lightweight, efficient classifier screens inbound messages, using minimal power, focused on catching potential threats.
- Stage 2: In-context analysis with our fine-tuned Gemma model, where we analyze a larger snapshot of the conversation to confirm a threat or discard a false alarm.
Built on strict governance
Presented at Singapore International Cyber Week (SICW 2026), this collaboration provides a model for messaging platforms balancing user protection with end-to-end encryption. Strict governance was maintained throughout development:
- Sovereign Sandbox: Fine-tuning took place within GovTech Singapore's managed and maintained GCP environment, keeping training data isolated.
- No Citizen Data: Training strictly excluded private or personally identifiable information, utilising anonymised datasets derived from scam reports and intelligence feeds.
- Stress-Testing: The model was tested against synthetic dialogues and local corpora to cover diverse scam categories and evolving impersonation tactics.
The future of on-device safety
The project demonstrates how AI can help counter criminality without compromising safety or privacy. It also shows how governments and model providers can work together to build tech for public good. With this lightweight, on-device model, we've proven the ability for local, real-time scam detection while ensuring chat interactions remain secure. We look forward to sharing more soon on our collaboration with the Singapore government, as well as exploring the potential for similar technology to be deployed in other countries.

content: As AI agents become participants in the development of their successors, they reshape both the production of intelligence and the role of human researchers. We introduce Atria Dawn Preview, a foundation agentic language model designed for scientific research and engineering workflows, with the goal of expanding the frontier of agent productivity in the real world. This model is trained via a Verifiable Experience Pipeline that connects tool-mediated interactions to executable environments and externally verified outcomes. Across 16 benchmarks spanning real-world research, engineering, and digital work, Atria Dawn Preview is competitive with frontier agents and achieves the highest reported score on five of them. Beyond standalone performance, we examine the real research-and-development process behind this model as a case study of human--AI collaboration, analyzing 769 task records from 56 participants together with agent logs. When asked to evaluate completed tasks under comparable conditions, participants rated about one-third of completed AI-assisted tasks as infeasible without AI. More strikingly, agents frequently propose methods and implement revisions, while humans retain most final decisions and guide exploration through judgment and feedback. These observations indicate a shift from task-level execution to project-level partnership, with human effort concentrating on what is worth pursuing and how evidence should guide research. Progress toward more autonomous AI research must therefore advance both the capacity for discovery and the capacity for meaningful human oversight, preserving accountable human authority over the risks and direction of continued development.

title: Simons Foundation launches $15M effort to help mathematicians navigate AI era
content:
Bringing people and ideas together to fund, conduct, and share transformative science.
Our grants advance knowledge and strengthen connections between science and society.
Discover the latest news, research, and updates.
We convene scientists, mathematicians, and thinkers to share ideas and explore new questions.
Founded by Jim and Marilyn Simons, we’re a private philanthropy advancing mathematics and basic science.
Work with us on the frontier of basic science research.
The Flatiron Institute is a research center that uses computational science to advance fields like physics, biology, and astronomy.
Search
The funding and resources will help researchers leverage AI tools and adapt to changes in the field.
The Simons Foundation today announced a new set of initiatives that will help the mathematics community navigate the rapid rise of artificial intelligence in the field.
Under a partnership, the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI will commit $15 million in combined funding and resources. The foundation will manage and award the funding, including through an open call for proposals, to support workshops and initiatives that help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results, learn and use new tools, share perspectives and shape collective standards for AI use.
“As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the research landscape, we want to help the mathematical community come together and forge the best path forward,” says Simons Foundation President David Spergel. “Now is the time to look at mathematics as a whole — not as a collection of proofs and theorems, but as a collective understanding driven by human curiosity.”
Anthropic and OpenAI will also provide AI tools and computing resources to researchers supported by the Simons Foundation, extending beyond mathematics to include basic science.
The awards and resources will be community-driven and leverage the foundation’s decades-long dedication to supporting and championing mathematics. The foundation was an early backer of machine learning for science, including funding the development of the Lean proof assistant, which has revolutionized how mathematicians work and made AI-assisted proofs possible. Additionally, the foundation has convened workshops, lectures and collaborations that have brought mathematicians together to explore and discuss AI’s role in the field.
“This is a moment for the mathematics community to come together,” Spergel says. “The community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, adopted and used, not any single company or institution. The goal of the program is to support the mathematics community.”

title: AI was great until it was not
content:
When I arrived at Oxford, I experienced what many would call a cultural shock. Beyond the flamboyant parties and visible micro-aggressions of the gowned elite, my physics and math courses felt radically different than before. The lectures were significantly more impersonal; the professors were a bit hostile; the crowd was huge, and everyone had something to prove. This would have felt rather normal if I had decided to continue my education in Argentina, but, instead, I had adapted to the American education model—at a school like Northwestern no less, which had a fairly small physics program. Not only that, I spent half of my undergraduate education surrounded by PhD students, taking the same classes as them.
But a masters in England was different. It felt bigger, more ominous. Most people opted to study and solve problem sets alone, and when we tried to work in groups there was an expectation to perform as the “genius” type. I had PhD offers from Harvard and Oxford straight from undergrad, and I felt like I had to prove I deserved it. It was partly my fault. I did feel the need to brag in order to be taken seriously, but it backfired on me. It was awkward at first, but the environment shifted drastically mid Michaelmas term. Pretty soon our discussions and ego games shifted from meaningless whiteboard debates to my classmates simply stating “I just asked ChatGPT how to do it.”
ChatGPT?
This was in late 2024. I had heard of AI in the past. Everyone was raving about it all year, but no one I knew had used it for class. I saw people complaining about how much water it used, how terrible it was for the environment and a few people even stated that it might kill us all someday. This felt like complete nonsense to me. I recall when I was writing my undergraduate thesis in mid-spring. I opened instagram to procrastinate for a few minutes, and I saw a popular “PhD influencer” (whatever that means) say she put her name in ChatGPT, and it blasted a lot of information about her and how great she was. I thought it was a bit scary for a “website” to pull up all your information like that (and I found the endeavour a bit narcissistic), but I was deeply curious, so I gave the chatbot a chance. I remember asking some question about scattering amplitudes, and it replied with nonsense. So, I pressed it and asked again with more detail, and it said:
“You should ask a theoretical physicist.”
And at that point, that was enough for me to close the window and never open it again.
That is, until a few months later, I was studying at Oxford with my “friends” at the time, and they kept raving about how ChatGPT could do their homework. Problem sets for most of the MMathPhys courses at Oxford are not graded. Real grades come from exams or your dissertation. A few classes require you to submit homework, but ‘passing’ is enough. I thought it was a bit meaningless to ask a chatbot to do everything for you when the entire purpose of the homework was to serve as exam practice. Yet, in January 2025, I found myself stuck trying to solve one QFT question, so I asked the chatbot like my friends recommended, and, again, it said some bullshit. I didn’t look at it again until a few months later.
It was a bit odd how the idea of “homework” had seemed to decay. Before, at least, we had the decency to look at Stack Overflow, and scout for similar problems or problem solving techniques that could help, but now suddenly people weren’t even doing that. They just asked ChatGPT to do everything. It defeated the purpose of doing homework to be honest. Though, I think we had lost that a while ago. I always thought that beyond practicing for the exam, problem sets were great to learn what collaboration during problem solving is like.
But in reality, collaboration has rarely been part of my reality as a student. The last time I recall truly collaborating with fellow students was in my freshman year of college. I was taking multivariable calculus with a bunch of engineering students. I knew two girls, Andrea and Juliana, from orientation and we immediately formed a small group chat to work together. We would try each problem set separately first, and then each of us would send our answers to the group chat and we would debate. For instance, one girl would ask me “oh, that’s a clever way to do this question. How did you know we had to integrate over this curve? Can you explain it to me?” or tell me “Hey, I think this question is wrong! You should use Lagrange multipliers this way instead.” And I would do the same thing for them. I learned a lot in that class, and I partly owed it to my great collaborators at the time. Debating, discussing and just learning from them was genuinely lovely. It helped me become better at math and truly grasp all the concepts.
I was deeply excited to start the physics major and collaborate with other physics peers. In the fall term of my sophomore year, I signed up for an honors differential equation math class with a friend who was also a physics major. As I thought was customary, we sent each other our solutions to check. It was my first time taking an honors math class, while that friend had taken three before. I also had to miss the first two lectures since my academic advisor insisted I wasn’t ready for honors, and I spent a week on a deeply boring standard class before I convinced the professor to let me switch. That is to say, I made a ton of mistakes in that first homework. So I messaged my friend like I had done in past and started asking: “Oh, it seems I misunderstood this concept, what do you mean here? Why is this true? I missed this class, so I thought we had to do something different” to which she accused me of trying to plagiarize her work and started ignoring me completely, and telling other people I was trying to copy her. Our friendship was never the same after that. And I learned a difficult lesson: I was alone. For the rest of the course, I worked on homework alone, I studied for exams alone, and I ended up with an A in the class. Actually, I spent most of my degree working alone, even as an undergrad among PhD students. I would explain my answers to my classmates, but I rarely had that back and forth from freshman year again.
That being said, ChatGPT just made the environment surrounding collaboration more bleak. Now, there was nothing beyond “Just ask ChatGPT.”
I was still hesitant to use AI. I saw many people in the MMathPhys use it for not only their homework, but for their dissertations and the research they expected to publish. I was confused. Another friend started using it as a therapist. I was still deeply confused. I was repelled by how agreeable it was, but it did give the weird illusion of having someone behind the screen.
Regardless, in May of 2025, all my bad decisions caught up to me. I actually spent most of my time at Oxford doing nothing. I always considered attending lectures some sort of social ritual. They have never helped me. I have always learned from books. Similarly, some problem sets were dense, uninsightful and useless, and if they were not needed for my grade, I wasn’t bothered to do them. I also had a PhD offer waiting for me at Harvard, so there was truly nothing to lose. I instead traveled a lot, went to parties, embarrassed myself, read a ton of books, played chess, fed the ducks and cried a lot. But at some point, I realized I had to get my masters degree and I had a month and a half to learn four Oxford MSc classes from scratch and pass my exams. I was cooked.
And there was ChatGPT. The thing about ChatGPT is that, well, it’s not a person. It doesn’t “think” like we do. But I realized it was very useful for one thing: rearranging what humans said in a more digestible way. So, I would sit with my cosmology and general relativity notes, and every time I got stuck or I couldn’t visualize a definition, I would just screenshot or copy the small section or sentence I did not understand and ChatGPT would re-explain it to me. Sometimes it included a quick example that helped me navigate index notation, for instance, or it would explain to me that torsion-free just meant that parallelograms closed.
One of the main incompatibilities with standard physics/math education and the way I think about problems is that definitions and derivations in a vacuum are a bit useless to me. I can follow complicated math and I can understand what a definition says, but it won’t click for me until I see a real illustrative example. This is not just a me thing. This is how Feynman thought about physics as well1, and I am sure a lot of people share this cognitive profile.
But instead of dealing with peers that got irritated at me and my stupid questions, ChatGPT provided that bridge almost instantly and with no fuss. After three weeks of using it, I realized I didn’t need it as much anymore. I could follow advanced concepts—like Penrose diagrams or Kerr Black Holes—on my own, make my own illustrative diagrams and derivations without AI. I took my exams two weeks after that. I learned the content General Relativity I&II, Cosmology and Geophysical Fluid Dynamics in a month and a half from scratch, while also taking the two Standard Model courses and a QFT in curved spacetimes class. My grades were between high passes and merits, but it was enough! I got my degree. And these were fully closed booked exams, so I did the work myself. But ChatGPT really helped me accelerate my knowledge acquisition.
That being said, I did not trust it at all for new research. Once I arrived to Harvard, I was given my first PhD project in early November of my G1 year, which is a bit early though not rare for high energy. I was working with a postdoc, and I was pleasantly surprised to see that the skills I learned in undergrad from my two mentors were incredibly useful for that problem. I embedded some twistor theory and chiral algebras into a nice mathematica notebook, which helped with a lot of calculations. I barely used AI on that project. It helped me find background literature and interpret some paragraphs/derivations in those papers. Beyond that, I only used Claude Opus to patch one piece of code in my library to help me deal with poles and residues in an expression because I wasn’t sure how to do it. That was it.
However, the single minus paper really changed the expectations surrounding AI in physics. Now, an internal model of OpenAI had found something researchers tried to work out for months before. That was cool, but it had nuance. A lot of the heavy lifting of that paper and the conceptual leaps were done by real people, but the accomplishment of AI was not to be understated. It was impressive. The proof was impressive and not straightforward, and this paper opened a lot of research directions in Celestial Holography. AI is actually great at proving things within a given framework. It’s also good at things that follow a strict logic or providing complex mathematical structures that are sound, but that’s not all that physics is. Or, I like to believe so.
The issue is that every time I showed my little mathematica notebook that I have coded mostly myself looking at the Wolfram documentation, both my seniors and PhD peers just would ask:
“Can’t ChatGPT do that?”
Maybe. But coding a problem in mathematica is not just about “efficiency” or writing fast code. It is about encoding a theory, a framework, working with corner cases, and learning. Maybe I could have asked Claude or ChatGPT to make a chiral algebras mathematica library, and it might have been good or better than mine, but then what would be the point? Maybe it would have been faster, slightly faster. Maybe I could have fed it all the different things I wanted to do, and let it code on the background and spit a ton of answers… but as a first year student that seemed to defeat the entire purpose of doing research in the first place. Furthermore, ChatGPT is not infallible. It can be very wrong. And not noticing when it’s wrong is just embarrassing for everyone involved.
I don’t believe in the grind of doing a difficult integral or proof from scratch to prove you are man enough to handle it (if a calculator or mathematica can do it, why suffer?), but I do think there is something valuable is solving an interesting problem, understanding a structure, and doing most of the conceptual heavy lifting. I finished my first project with very limited AI use, and the paper was published.
But when it was time to start my second project as a fresh G2, I did notice the environment had changed drastically. If you walk across the Harvard physics department and lean into the offices, a lot of people will have ChatGPT, Codex, Claude or similar open in their monitors. A lot of the emails I started to receive contained AI generated notes or notes based on ideas given by ChatGPT. It wasn’t just me, a lot of my peers go through this too, here and everywhere. This is a common experience now. Now, “brainstorming” means talking to ChatGPT. A lot of my time is spent deciphering ChatGPT notes, realizing it’s nonsense, and moving on to the next.
I was annoyed. I had objections, questions, and concerns, but I was shut down and told to ask ChatGPT. So, I asked ChatGPT and it just “validated” everything I said, but didn’t propose any solutions. The problem is that I wanted to debate with my superiors, ask questions… and I couldn’t. I realized a lot of doing a PhD in theoretical physics is dealing with loud people screaming at a blackboard, so it doesn’t feel very interactive either. Some people say a lot of fancy words. Bullshitting is common practice some say. I realized at some point that it wasn’t just me; there was some posturing, some performance, and ChatGPT made that worse. So, I was alone with a chatbot again. But, now, I didn’t have a set of lecture notes written by a top physicist at Cambridge about a theory that was established almost a century ago… I had a couple of papers, vague ideas, and nowhere to go because on a PhD you work out things no one has done before.
And it wasn’t good. Because I am just a second year PhD student and I don’t know anything. I know a lot of things, but in the grand scheme of things, I am inexperienced and I need mentors. And a chatbot cannot be my mentor. And then I realized that same tool that helped me so much a year ago was drowning me and my field. I don’t think technologies are evil, but I do think how humans utilize some technologies can be harmful. But it’s not AI’s fault, it’s ours.
I did realize early on that a lot of people in my field were less focused on finding the truth than they were on projecting, being right and showing off. I realized early on that for a lot of physicists teaching and mentorship is more of a burden than something they deem particularly valuable. We want the fastest PhD students, the ones that published three papers in undergrad, the ones that finish a calculation the fastest. We want the hottest topics and the most citations. But if a chatbot can replace a PhD student, if it’s faster, more efficient and it can absorb Weinberg’s QFT volumes in five minutes, why do we need students at all?
Why do we collaborate when we can just work alone with a bot?
Remember when I mentioned I had that group chat with my engineering friends and we were constantly comparing and brainstorming? Sometimes, they would catch a concept or see a clean solution I didn’t notice, and I would do that for them too. That helped us grow, and it gave me a deep understanding of a lot of those concepts. I would solve exams in unexpected ways, but that was fun! It helped truly grasp the math and how beautiful it was. But that was also a healthy collaboration. It wasn’t about getting the highest grade, or having the smartest solution, gatekeeping or screaming. We would sit down, try it out, politely discuss, and explain. We wouldn’t be mean or condescending, we would just learn from each other and improve each other.
People keep us in check. Each person is different. We all have a different background, a different way of seeing the world. We come from different training. But, you learn from others and they learn from you too.
And we are losing that now too. Should we fear that colleagues working in AI companies might take our prompts and try to get ahead to solve a problem before we do? Should we fear for threats? Should we fear that our days as PhD students will be spent telling a machine to “try harder” instead of deeply understanding something new?
Truth is, I was very impressed and excited about how ChatGPT helped me study. Would I rather have responsive professors, lecturers that know pedagogy, physicists that want to write understandable papers instead of purposefully burying insight in meaningless jargon, and peers I can talk to without having an anxiety spike? Yes. I would rather have that one hundred percent. And I fear that now, it’s all going to be worse. Because we now have in our hands a machine that validates all of our biases and buries them in dozens of pages of meaningless math.
I am just a PhD student who feels a little defeated, not because AI might take my job, I am privileged enough for that to not be a concern (and let’s be honest, I am privileged enough to have the opportunity to do a PhD in theoretical physics). But because the way we are using AI is destroying what made science fun in the first place. Is it really fun to publish thirty papers in a week using AI just for the sake of it? One of my friends in the program rightfully asks “Are those papers worth publishing?”
The entire point of solving an interesting problem or understanding the mysteries of the universe is not to win an award or have the most citations, but to get closer to that almost mythical thing we call truth, to know the universe and ourselves through the study of the nature of things.
The problem is that the little chatbot in our pockets is making us more isolated and in so, it’s making us stray further from this humble goal: to learn. But it wasn’t just the chatbot, it was the culture around academia too. I think chatbots are a mirror, a deeply validating sycophantic mirror with the knowledge of the internet. But mirrors can be dangerous if we stay for too long too charmed by our own reflection, and we forget about everything and everyone else too. In particular, it would be pretty sad to destroy one of the few things that makes our life meaningful, not the fancy prize or the fancy position, but simply having a community to share and discuss and learn. To learn things. That is a beautiful thing.
-Nia
"If men could only see the cause, and why
This mountain of distress weighs down the mind,
They’d drop all else and study to find out
The Universe’s Nature and its layout—
Since it’s our status for eternity
That is at issue here, and not just one
Brief hour—the state in which all mortals must
Spend time to come, when once our days are done."
-Lucretius2
Lucretius, T. C. (2007). The nature of things (A. E. Stallings, Trans.). Penguin Books. (Original work published ca. 50 B.C.E.

title: Apertus 1.5 Release Notes
content:
Apertus 1.5 Release Notes
Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.
Key Enhancements
- Native Multimodal Understanding: Apertus 1.5 accepts images and audio alongside text, bringing documents, diagrams, and photos into the conversation. The models can also process spoken language, though this remains experimental.
- Thinking Mode: The models can be switched into a thinking mode to reason about the input before answering, which improves performance on reasoning problems.
- Long Context: The context window grows to 262,144 tokens, a 4x increase over Apertus 1.0.
- Improved Instruction-Following: Better instruction adherence than Apertus 1.0 gives more predictable and accurate responses.
- Improved Tool Use: The models are trained for better tool integration, allowing more effective use of external tools and APIs.
- Open Values: Stronger adherence to the Apertus Charter, which brings transparency to the model’s values and principles.
Training Process
The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline
Multimodality Through the Tokenizer
We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.
Pre-Training
Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:
- Unpaired: text plus standalone images and audio, so the model learns the new modalities.
- Paired: image–caption and audio–transcript pairs, so it aligns them with language.
- Cooldown: higher-quality data with more math and code.
- Long context: the window grows step by step from 8k to 262k tokens.
Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.
Post-Training
Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).
- SFT on 3.7M text samples plus image and speech data. Reasoning traces are added only to prompts the model can't already solve without them. Tool-use data is restricted to execution-verified trajectories. We release the text SFT mix we used on Hugging Face.
- Long-context SFT at the full 262k window restores the long-context ability that short-context SFT erodes.
- RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on about 350k math, code, instruction-following, multilingual, and vision prompts, mixing thinking on and off.
- DPO with judge-scored preference pairs improves chat quality, tool use, and safety. We release the preference pool and training pairs.
- SDPO aligns the model with the Apertus Charter through judge feedback and self-distillation.
Evaluation Results
Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.
The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.
While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.
We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).
Evaluation Cards: Apertus ❤️ EvalEval
Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.
The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.
Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.
We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.
Apertus 1.5 Reproducibility
All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.
The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

| Supervised finetuning (SFT) | Apertus-v1.5-8B-SFT | Apertus-v1.5-70B-SFT | 
| Reinforcement learning (RLVR) | Apertus-v1.5-8B-RLVR | Apertus-v1.5-70B-RLVR | 
| Preference alignment (DPO) | Apertus-v1.5-8B-DPO | Apertus-v1.5-70B (final) |

| SDPO (charter alignment, 8B only) | gretelai/gretel-safety-alignment-en-v1 | self-distillation | 
Model Availability
Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.
Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.
Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.
How to Get Involved
Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.
In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.
If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!
