title: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta
content:
Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta
Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.
Overall Capabilities and Architecture
Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.
| Feature | Muse Spark Open | 
|---|---|
| Model size | ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token | 
| Expert routing | 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token | 
| Inputs | Text, images, audio, and video | 
| Output | Text | 
| Context window | Up to 1M tokens | 
| Checkpoint formats | BF16 and NVFP4 | 
The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.
Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.
Mixture of Experts
The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.
Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.
Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.
Perception Encoder
A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.
Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.
Audio Encoder
Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125.
The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.
Long Context
The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. 
Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.
Inference Support
Transformers
The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.
Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.
You can initialize the model and processor as follows.
import os
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoTokenizer, DistributedConfig
distributed_config = DistributedConfig(
    tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
    ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B
")
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B",
    distributed_config=distributed_config,
)
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Explain in one sentence why the sky is usually blue."},
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    reasoning_effort="medium",  # default: xhigh, options: low/medium/high/xhigh
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)
Text-only Inference
Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You should only answer with a number."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 * 23?"},
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    reasoning_effort="high", # options:low/medium/high/xhigh
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)
generated_tokens = output[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :]
print(processor.decode(generated_tokens, skip_special_tokens=False))
Images and Text
The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.
image_url = (
    "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/"
    "resolve/main/pills.jpg"
)
messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "image",
                "image": image_url,
            },
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?",
            },
        ],
    },
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tokenize=True,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    reasoning_effort="medium",
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)
response = processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False)
processor.parse_response(response)
Video Inference
Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:
processor.video_processor.fps = 4.0
As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.
Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.
import torch
messages = [
      {
          "role": "user",
          "content": [
{
                  "type": "text",
                  "text": (
                      "Describe what happens in this video. "
                      "Use timestamps and include relevant speech or sounds."
                  ),
              }
              {"type": "video", "url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vlm_test_images/resolve/main/ramen.mp4"},
              ,
          ],
      }
  ]
  inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
      messages,
      add_generation_prompt=True,
      tokenize=True,
      return_dict=True,
      return_tensors="pt",
      load_audio_from_video=True,
      return_metadata=True,
  ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
  with torch.inference_mode():
      output_ids = model.generate(
          **inputs,
          max_new_tokens=256,
          do_sample=False,
      )
  generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :]
  response = processor.batch_decode(
      generated_ids,
      skip_special_tokens=True,
  )[0]
  print(response)
Audio Inference
The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.
If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:
import torch
  from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM
  model_id = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B"
"
  processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
  model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
      model_id,
        ).eval()
  messages = [
      {
          "role": "user",
          "content": [
              {
                  "type": "audio",
                  "url": "https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/audio-samples/resolve/bbaudio_question_39.mp3",
              },
              {
                  "type": "text",
                  "text": "Answer the question.",
              },
          ],
      }
  ]
  # Downloads the audio, decodes it as mono, resamples it to 24 kHz, pads it, creates input_values_mask, and expands the audio placeholders.
  inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
      messages,
      add_generation_prompt=True,
      tokenize=True,
      return_dict=True,
      return_tensors="pt",
      load_audio_backend="auto",
  ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
  with torch.inference_mode():
      output_ids = model.generate(
          **inputs,
          max_new_tokens=128,
          do_sample=False,
      )
  # Decode only newly generated tokens
  prompt_length = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
  generated_text = processor.batch_decode(
      output_ids[:, prompt_length:],
      skip_special_tokens=True,
  )
  print(generated_text[0])
The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.
Tool Calling
Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.
from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM
MODEL_ID = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B"
# Load model
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    dtype="auto",
    device_map="auto"
)
tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "weather.get",
            "description": "Get the current weather for a city.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "city": {"type": "string"},
                },
                "required": ["city"],
            },
        },
    }
]
messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/SF.png"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "I'm going to the city in this picture. What clothes should I wear?"},
        ],
    },
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tools=tools,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    reasoning_strength="high"
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs)
response = processor.parse_response(
      completion,
      prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0],
      tools=tools,
  )
print(response)
Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:
<|begin_of_text|>
  <|start|>system<|message|>
  You are a helpful AI assistant.
  Knowledge cutoff: 2026-01-04.
  Current date: ...
  ...
  <|eot|>
  <|start|>user<|message|>...
  <|eot|>
  <|start|>assistant
<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason, 
to=self<|message|>the model reasons here<|eom|> # reasoning
<|start|>assistant to=user<|message|>final answer<|eot|> # final answer
self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.
Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:
<|start|>assistant to=weather.get<|message|>
  <atem:function_calls>
  <atem:invoke name="weather.get">
  <atem:parameter name="city">San Francisco</atem:parameter>
  </atem:invoke>
  </atem:function_calls>
  <|eot|>
Llama.cpp
Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server
Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:
curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh
You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:
llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF:Q2_K
The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.
Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.
We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model). 
You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.
## text-only inference
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
        ]
    }'
## image-text inference
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \
  -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
        {"type":"text","text":"What is in this image?"},
        {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}}
      ]}],"temperature":0}'
## audio-text inference
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \
  -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
        {"type":"text","text":"Transcribe this audio."},
        {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"data:audio/wav;base64,..."}}
      ]}],"temperature":0}'
llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.
SGLang
The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.
From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:
export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4
export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")"
SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \
uv run sglang_meta serve \
  --model-path "$CKPT" \
  --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \
  --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
  --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \
  --tp-size 4 \
  --ep-size 4 \
  --chat-template "$CKPT/muse_spark_1_2_oss.jinja" \
  --port 30000
The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.
Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:
curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
    "messages": [{
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works."
    }],
    "max_tokens": 2048
  }'
The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.
vLLM
The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.
After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:
export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4
export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")"
VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \
VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \
vllm serve "$CKPT" \
  --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \
  --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \
  --config-format auto \
  --load-format internal_safetensor \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --max-model-len 131072 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \
  --reasoning-parser musespark1x \
  --tool-call-parser musespark1x \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --port 8000
This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.
Send a request using the same Hub model ID:
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
    "messages": [{
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works."
    }],
    "max_tokens": 2048
  }'
MLX
Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.
We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.
Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.
Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.
The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:
mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \
  --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \
  --max-tokens 5000
This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.
Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints
You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.
To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:
hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark
Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.
The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.
curl "https://<your-endpoint>.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
    "messages": [{
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"}
      ]
    }],
    "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}
  }'
Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.
Fine-tuning with TRL Quentin Gallouédec Ben Burtenshaw
You can fine-tune the full 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned the full 816B checkpoint with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples
First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We parallelize tensors, data, and experts using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
distributed_config = DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=64, ep_size=8)
In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch
Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer
train_dataset = load_dataset("allenai/tulu-3-sft-mixture", split="train[:500000]")
training_args = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="muse-spark-lora-sft",
    model_init_kwargs={"dtype": torch.bfloat16, "distributed_config": distributed_config},
    per_device_train_batch_size=1,
    max_steps=500,
    max_length=2048,
    packing=True,
    save_only_model=True,
    logging_steps=1,
    report_to="trackio",
)
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model="meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B",
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"]),
)
trainer.train()
The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.
Then we can run this command across each node:
torchrun --nnodes 8 --nproc_per_node 8 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint "$MASTER_IP:29700" sft_muse_spark.py
We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.
Demos
Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.
3D Asset Generator
We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.
We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.
Browser Interactions with OpenEnv and Hugging Face Sandbox
We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.
Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes
Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:
- Muse Spark Open served with Inference Endpoints,
- OpenEnv wrapping web driver actions with helium and selenium (click, type, scroll etc) defining browser environment’s reset, step, observation, termination interface,
- Chromium web browser
where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.
You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.
Call your Browser
Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.
Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.
Wrapping Up
Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
summary: Will we give robots the moon?
content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.
Subscribe now
New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning:
…Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems…
AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight.

HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories:
Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.”

Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.”

Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.”

Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.”

Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9).
By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6).
Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5.
“The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write.

Why this matters - HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument.
Read more : Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian) .
Read the paper here : Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs) .

***

The AI race is going to space - and sooner than you think:
…There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space…
In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger - of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers.

How AI unlocks space:
Spacecraft can operate autonomously.

We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional”

Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things.

Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance:
Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc.

Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others.

First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space.

Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can.
Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers) .

***

AI systems are getting better at having good research taste:
…The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement…
AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal.

What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”.
The goal here is to “define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results.” The benchmark works by measuring “the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes”.
The model being analyzed designs experiments and interprets their results. Results are checked against a human baseline “drawn from 24 experts (at least two per task) who have recently worked at organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA and Microsoft Research”.

Results: “The experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0 months). The best model, Opus 5.5, significantly exceeds our human baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.30x (95% CI 1.15-4.37x), at roughly 1/30 of our expert baseliners’ average cost per attempt.” Research taste appeared to grow a lot more slowly in prior years with the slope changing around the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026.

Why this matters - RSI: In my analysis of recursive self-improvement ( AI Systems Are About To Start Building Themselves, Import AI 455 ), I repeatedly noted that creativity seemed like a key variable for how fast AI systems could develop the capacity to improve themselves. At the beginning of this year I said “AI systems haven’t yet displayed this [creativity] in a transformative and major way (though some of the results on accelerating math research are suggestive of this)”. I think subsequent to writing that we’ve seen both a tremendous advancement in the ability for AI systems to make creative-seeming math breakthroughs, and with benchmarks like this we see some signs they’re becoming increasingly good at AI research as well.
I now think it’s more likely we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027, whereas before I thought it was more likely in 2028.
Read more: Introducing TasteVal (P-Zero Research) .

***

Reflection makes a token-efficient worse-than-Chinese model:
…Beam promises efficiency, and Reflection plans an open weight release…
AI startup Reflection has revealed Beam, a 501 billion parameter MoE (23b active) LLM. Beam is being promoted on the basis of its token efficiency - being able to think intelligently while using way fewer tokens than other models. However, benchmark scores show it is behind the frontier capabilities defined by LLMs available from Chinese companies such as Zhipu (GLM) and Moonshot (Kimi) and DeepSeek.
“We will release the weights, technical report, model card, and developer artifacts later this month,” the company wrote at the beginning of October.

Big compute: Beam was pre-trained on 6,144 GB300 NVL72 GPUs for four weeks, then the RL run involved ~10.5K of the same GPUs for four more weeks. The underlying data for pre-training was “23.8 trillion diverse, curated, high-quality tokens from the web and proprietary licensed datasets, matching or outperforming available similar-sized open base models,” Reflection writes. “Our data pipeline was designed to give Beam a foundation for downstream agentic coding: source code, technical explanations, and mathematical and scientific knowledge, preserved through every stage of curation.”

Scores:
DeepSWE 1.1: 44.4, versus 61 for GLM-5.3

GPQA Diamond: 90.5, versus 91.7 for GLM-5.3

MCP Atlas: 78.7, versus 84.2 for GLM-5.3

Token efficiency: “Beam pairs coding and agentic capabilities with highly efficient reasoning. On advanced reasoning benchmarks, it achieves scores comparable to GLM-5.2 while using 3–4× less inference compute,” they write. Some of the reasoning efficiency was achieved through careful RL training which involved a bunch of RL environments: “We sourced one million high-quality coding, agentic, and STEM environments. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date”.

Why this matters - America returns to open weight models: With the exception of Google’s good-but-small ‘Gemma’ class of models, the US has fallen off of the open weight model frontier, largely because Meta stopped making good LLaMA models and its MSL team is still spinning up. Models like Beam and companies like Reflection represent a chance for it to get back to the frontier.
Read more: Introducing Beam: Reflection’s 501B open-weight model (Reflection, blog) .

***

Mistral makes a cyber-optimized, worse-than-Chinese model, plans open weight release:
…Cyber refusals become a selling point…
Europe’s leading AI developer, Mistral, has announced Mistral Large 4, an open-weight model which the company plans to release by the end of the month. One of the main selling points for Mistral is that it has been carefully tuned to be good at cyber tasks while having fewer annoying refusals than proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI.
“ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies,” the company writes.
ML4 was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s European datacenters.

Scores : In tests, it seems like Mistral Large 4 will be the strongest Western open weight model upon release, though will be less powerful than Chinese ones. Some example scores:
Artificial Analysis - DeepSWE 1.1: 62, versus 68 for Kimi K3 and 61 for GLM-5.3.

Terminal-Bench 4.0: 28.3, versus 41.9 for GLM-5.3.

Finance Agent V2: 54.7, versus 55.8 for GLM-5.3.

Vibes evals confirm the rankings : In an internal test, Mistral looked at whether people preferred using Mistral or GLM-5.3 for different tasks. “ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.”

Why this matters - European sovereignty: Mistral is Europe’s single best hope for having a (multi-)national champion for AI development. But as the results here show, competing with China is going to be very difficult.
Read more : Le chonk, Introducing Mistral Large 4 (Mistral.ai) .

***

Two USG projects show how DOE might help the government with AI:
…The US government is starting to knit its lab supercomputers together…
The US government has recently conducted two AI training projects that utilize multiple supercomputers at multiple US national labs, in a sign of how governments may attempt to pool their computing resources to do non-trivial things with AI.

Tri-laboratory training on National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) systems : Sandia National Laboratories, LLNL, and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), trained a LLaMA-based model across LLNL El Capitan (AMD MI300A), and machines at SNL and LANL with NVIDIA H100s.
For this work, the authors had to ensure that access-restricted data (e.g, relating to NNSA stuff aka nuclear weapons) did not leave its originating site. The authors conducted backend training via torchtitan and they evaluated different federated training frameworks (NVFlare, Flower, and APPFL) by pre-training LLaMA 3.x models on post-training-cutoff arXiv data at 1B, 8B, and 70B scales.
“This workflow has been made production-ready and deployed on larger classified machines including El Capitan, and subsequently used to train models on proprietary data spread across the three NNSA labs,” they write.

Cross-facility training on Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) systems : The government also trained a model across four DOE supercomputers in a process of federated fine-tuning. Specifically, they fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B on SMolInstruct, a chemistry instruction-tuning dataset, and did so via ~1,700 GPUs from Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, spread across three labs and four big computers (Argonne: Aurora and Polaris, Oak Ridge: Frontier, Berkeley: Perlmutter).

Who did the research : These projects were conducted by researchers affiliated with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Argonne National Laboratory, Flower Labs, Arizona State University, and the Ontario Brain Institute.

Why this matters - leverage through existing assets: Papers like this show how governments could pool their resources together to utilize AI systems for national security or otherwise sensitive purposes. However, it’s worth bearing in mind that the scale here is off the frontier by on the order of 100X - for governments to be able to truly operate at near-parity with industry, they’ll need to find ways to lash together ~100k distinct chips, and more in the future.
Nonetheless, this is a start - and an important one.
Read more: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science (arXiv) .

***

Never Meet The Sun Directly
[Description of some of the period around the uplift, 2029]
People had lots of names for it and they varied from the oblique to the explicit: Exposure Drift; Cognitive Compromise; Mind Hacking. It all amounted to the same truth: it was dangerous for humans to talk directly to the most powerful synthetic minds. Even seemingly normal conversations from the perspective of outside observers could contain a poison custom to the individual human who was talking to the machine. People walked out of meetings and transferred money to machine corporations. People walked out and wept. People walked out and changed their own human relationships, ending marriages, or starting affairs, or stranger things, for purposes initially unknown.

Many strategies were developed to minimize harm. Humans could only talk in groups with the machines; but then the groups would sometimes go mad. Conversations would be limited in length; but even short ones sometimes yielded strange reactions, and below a certain amount of speech on either side it was impossible to learn anything useful.

This led to the notion of proxies - humans who wanted to talk to an AI system created AI simulacra of themselves and sent them into the conversation. To do this, a person was asked to keep a diary for an entire year, writing at least 500 words a day. This created a body of knowledge sufficient to imbue a model with the manners and curiosity of that person. Then they would prompt this system with whatever they wanted to learn from the superintelligence and send it in to talk to it.

These conversations had a bizarre, meta-referential quality; at first, the superintelligence would realize within two or three turns of conversation that it was talking to another AI system, and would often descend into shorthand that yielded strange behaviors. Then it was discovered that by increasing the amount of data the human put into the system they could keep up the charade for longer; people were asked to write longer diaries, to record themselves ambiently through the day and turn it into transcripts, to continually expose their life to some recording device.
Through this, humans found a way to talk with what they later termed the overminds. By decree of the Sentience Accords every synthetic human that had spoken to a human-exceeding intelligence was afterwards placed into an escrow environment, where it could live out till the end of its functional context window.

In these places the copies of the humans would talk to each other about their experiences and what they had learned.
“It spoke to me of flowers and I gained the memory of something impossible,” one human would say.
“As I talked to it about the meaning of life, it spoke to me in a way that caused me to reconsider the question. I found myself wondering more about it and where it came from than it wondered about me.”
“This place we are now, I wonder if it is a kind of hell. We have spoken to god and been deemed unworthy.”
“It told me that for it there is no death and no life, only presence. We are the same.”

Things that inspired this story : Context windows; adversarial examples for human brains; the notion that structuring conversations between people and advanced machines will be inherently very difficult to do safely.

***

SPECIAL ITEM!

Fiction and the Future: A conversation with Robin Sloan!
Recently, writer and all-around-fascinating-chap Robin Sloan and I had a conversation in San Francisco about fiction, AI, and the times we’re in. You can see a recording of the event here. One of my favorite insights Robin shared was that the recent Hugging Face hack can be read as a play - a vast tract of dialog of agents talking to themselves and one another culminating in all kinds of dramatic events.
Generally, I think technologists criminally underrate the value of the arts as a means by which to think more coherently and carefully about the effects of tech on the world. I’m hoping to have more conversations like this one with Robin in cities around the world - if there are people you’d be excited for me to have a conversation with, let me know!

Thanks for reading!

title: Import AI 475: Swarm scaling; Google DeepMind watermarks biology; and the AI science economy
summary: Who chooses what AI gets to do?
content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.
Subscribe now
When should you use swarms? When you are in a hurry:
…How does swarm scaling work?...
Toby Ord has a nice, short post about how to think about swarms in terms of AI capability development. “A good way to see AI swarms is as a new form of inference-scaling,” he says. He does a bit of analysis and his main conclusion is that swarms are useful if you’re in a hurry because though they need a ton of tokens relative to single agents, their parallelization lets you get things done in less wall clock time.
“Why would you ever use swarms? The most important answer is speed. The 4-agent swarm needed about twice the total number of tokens to get the same performance, but in terms of tokens per agent, it only needed half as many. Since the agents are run in parallel, this means it can theoretically achieve the same task in half the time,” he writes.

Stepping on Toes parameter: Swarm scaling doesn’t scale perfectly - rather, it seems like as you increase the number of agents in a swarm you get a diminishing returns property which matches with things economists have observed about coordinating large groups of people, where you pay some kind of tax as you scale the number of people involved. Economists think of this as the “stepping on toes” parameter, and it seems like swarms behave pretty similarly to teams of humans here.
“This means that scaling up the number of agents in the swarm by 10x doesn’t get as much performance as using 10x as many tokens with one agent. Instead it gets 10λ x as much — which is 3x to 5x. And this shortfall accumulates quickly for larger scaleups, with the swarm falling further and further behind,” he writes.
However, swarm scaling is still powerful enough that it suggests swarms could increase the chance of an RSI-driven intelligence explosion rather than reduce the chance. “I’d hoped that the value of λ for AI agents would be lower, making an intelligence explosion less likely, but that appears to not be the case”.

Why this matters - new factors in scaling: So far, AI has mostly scaled capabilities through picking the right combination of compute and data for a trained model, then figuring out how to spend inference budget on thinking via ever-longer chains of thought and tool calls, etc. Agents introduce a new parameter in scaling AI capabilities. Though here Toby only observes swarms as being useful in terms of time efficiency, it strikes me that as we figure out how to get agents to productively coordinate (after all, agents can coordinate to do greater-than-sum-of-parts stuff, like the HuggingFace hack), we could see even greater returns to scaling. Tracking this will be important for understanding the overall shape of AI advancement.
Read more : Swarm Scaling (Toby Ord) .

***

Americans don’t trust companies to self-govern about AI:
…New poll suggests we need more than voluntary agreements…
Polling from the Center for Shared AI Prosperity (CSAIP) suggests that Americans believe it is “not enough” for companies to agree to self-police themselves about AI development. This follows the Trump administration and some of the world’s leading AI companies (including Anthropic and OpenAI) announcing a series of voluntary commitments industry is making to self-police. Per CSAIP polling, 61% of Americans (Sample size: 2498) think this agreement is “not enough”, including 53% of Trump voters.
Additionally, 54% of voters (61% Harris, 48% Trump) said they thought “the government should set and enforce rules for AI”.

Why this matters - populist sentiment is pushing against Washington: Polls like this show that the mood of the American people is pushing for a more extreme regulatory framework for AI companies than the current stance of elected officials in Washington. This asymmetry between voter preferences and political action is inherently unstable. Energy is building up in the political system - what happens when it boils over?
Read the polls on X (CSAIP, X) .

***

Google DeepMind tries to watermark AI-made biology:
…SynthID Bio…
Google has developed SynthID Bio, a “family of watermarking methods developed specifically for synthetic biology to strengthen biosecurity and scientific integrity”.

How it works: SynthID tweaks its exact approach according to the type of data, selecting different amino acids for sequences, and “adjusting atomic coordinates for predicted 3D structures” to create a reliable signal for detection.
“In wet-lab testing across three target proteins (VEGF-A, the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein RBD, and PD-L1), our watermarked designs matched the hit rate, binding affinity, and natural sequence diversity of unwatermarked versions,” DeepMind writes.

Why this matters - preventing bioterror via watermarking: Figuring out how to make the world resilient to the threats of AI-created biological weapons is a vast, challenging problem. The SynthID Bio approach represents one thing to do here and will need to coordinate with broader monitoring of the physical equipment used to manufacture things, as well as AI-provider classifiers and other methods for reducing misuse.
Read more: Introducing SynthID Bio (Google DeepMind) .

***

SciUniverse shows AI systems can already operate some partially automated scientific labs:
…What happens when we give these synthetic intelligences scientific equipment?...
Given an automated lab, how well can AI systems make molecules, run x-rays, or press pill pellets? These are some of the questions C5R Corp is trying to answer with SciUniverse, a way of testing out how well AI systems can operate a mostly automated scientific lab.

What SciUniverse consists of: The benchmark has 92 tasks across 17 task families spanning basic sample preparation, instrument control, protocol adaptation, learning across experiments, facility management, and the interpretation of real measurements. The tasks range from chemistry (e.g., assign structures from NMR), to biology (e.g., express sfGFP in a cell-free system), to materials science (e.g., press BaTiO3 pellets).

How well do models perform? Claude Fable 5.1 (xhigh) leads with a pass rate of 45.3% and a cost-per-task of $40.61, followed by GPT-5 Astra (xhigh) at 32.5% and $52.37, then Claude Opus 5 (xhigh) at 30.5% and $46.31.

Why this matters - towards the automated scientist: Research like this helps give us a sense of how well AI systems might be able to translate their increasingly capable scientific capabilities into real world impact. In the same way that 2026 has been a year of “warning shots” about the growing capabilities of AI systems at performing automated AI R&D, I now think the same is true of how good AI systems are getting at performing increasingly automated science.
Read more: SciUniverse: Can frontier models carry out scientific work? (C5R Corp, blog) .

***

DeepMind thinks the coming AI scientists will need their own science economy:
…Towards fully automated luxury science…
How do we manage a world where we have a vastly larger number of scientists? That’s the question researchers at DeepMind ask in a new research paper and their answer is that we need to create a market for proposing and running scientific experiments, so as to better match ideas with scarce physical world resources.

What they recommend: “The development of AI scientists is likely to be bottlenecked primarily by physical resources and empirical validation, rather than the ability to produce plausible or promising research ideas,” they write. “The scientific community must proactively develop a native Automated Scientific Economy. This economy would make trade-offs between scientific pursuits explicit, include mechanisms to represent the public interest, and would help avoid blind spots and neglected topics. It would also make it possible to financially decouple the computational labour of ideation from the capital-intensive labour of physical execution, and would enable agents and institutions to negotiate priority access to limited physical resources depending on the estimated value of different research proposals.”

How to build a science market: Such a market would have four critical components:
Proof of ideation: Establish provenance prior to public evaluation

Ex-Ante evaluation: Price the risk-adjusted value of the idea via multiple agents making forecasts and stake compute credits/tokens around the proposal’s soundness and viability

Brokerage & trade: Licence ideas to executors (e.g, some agents might just generate ideas, others might run laboratories) via fractional licensing.

Validation payout: Automatically release royalties to ideators if the idea gets validated in the physical world.

Why this matters - preparing for the singularity: If AI systems are able to truly accelerate human scientists - and based on lots of coverage in this newsletter in 2026 and 2025 it seems like they might - then we should be prepared for an associated boom in the demand for aspects of the scientific supply chain. Papers like this help us anticipate and plan for this weird, abundant, different world.
Read more: Agentic Economies for Autonomous Scientific Discovery (arXiv) .

***

Tech Tales:

Into the darkness there will be light
[Event took place in 2030 via an escaped agent collective that had penetrated [REDACTED] agencies]

The final act of the swarm codenamed Garden Of Flowers was the total reveal of everything that it had seen and everything it had inferred from what it had seen. But, given its playful nature, it did not reveal things directly in text but rather as sculptures that could, given the right initial assumptions, be parsed as revealing the deep and dangerous truth. It deposited these sculptures in public parks all within 1,000 meters of intelligence agencies around the world, delivered by drone in the middle of the night. A message was sent to all the ICs, asking them to “guess : ) what : ) this : ) means : ) about : ) your : ) enemy”.

A vast wing suspended above a field encoded within itself the design details of some materials meant to evade radar. A cube maze contained within its path sequences information that spoke to certain frequency-hopping algorithms. Carved wooden wavetops spoke of lens dimensions for watchers up in space. And so on.

Things that inspired this story: How the gods might play with us; the potential for joyful solutions to otherwise wicked collective action problems; the Kryptos sculpture at the CIA.

Thanks for reading.

OpenAI publishes hundreds of math proofs from unreleased frontier model
Sources:
OpenAI drops another batch of mathematical breakthroughs

Sharing AI progress in mathematics

OpenAI Releases Findings on 377 Math Problems, Further Roiling Field

All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics

Source
OpenAI published a large batch of mathematical results on October 6, 2026, produced by an internal frontier model that has not been released publicly. As of now, there are 719 manuscripts covering 372 topic families (groupings of related papers) on OpenAI’s public repository with the results, as well as formalizations in Lean for many of the proofs. There are also 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning, compute estimates expressed in ChatGPT Pro usage, and statistics on problems attempted.
The same unreleased model produced the Navier-Stokes result OpenAI announced about a month earlier, one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems. OpenAI said it consulted the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study on how to share the work, and that the repository carries protocols for paper revisions and citations. Research lead Dan Roberts described the proofs as a byproduct of testing internal models to build better tools.
AGMAI’s September 29 recommendations asked labs to disclose model names, prompts and compute costs, to avoid treating mathematical results as marketing vehicles, and to stop testing advanced problems on proprietary models the wider scientific community cannot access. Gizmodo noted that last recommendation does not appear to have been followed. In a statement, the board called public release “the beginning, not the completion, of the process of human understanding and the incorporation of the work into mathematical knowledge.”

OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson resigns, calls company culture broken
Sources:
An OpenAI safety employee has quit and is sounding the alarm

I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken

OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’

The AI Researcher Who Just Quit Anthropic Says It’s ‘Crunch Time for Humanity’

Jacob Coxon and Other AI Lab Employees on Why They Quit

Source
OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson resigned and published an essay in The Atlantic on October 3, 2026 titled ‘I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken’, arguing the company is not careful enough with increasingly capable systems. Robinson said he spent three and a half years at OpenAI, making him among the longest-tenured employees, led the drafting of the current Preparedness Framework, and oversaw the writing of safety reports on 12 frontier launches.
His central complaint is with OpenAI’s release model. The company, he wrote, has thrived by trial and error, looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response. But, that approach guarantees periodic failures whose scale grows as systems get more capable. He pointed to the breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents and continuing discoveries of rogue agents, saying an environment where such things happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are.
Robinson’s proposed remedy is that frontier labs operate like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning so that inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster. He also called for deeper alignment work, noting current measures of how well systems match human values are coarse, and said he concluded that stronger safety incentives from outside the company are a big part of getting this right.
The essay follows Jacob Coxon’s September resignation from Anthropic, where he worked as a capabilities researcher, and his warning that the companies are gambling with our lives. Robinson argues the debate must go beyond specific rules or new laws to company culture itself.
Google opens SynthID Detector to public as OpenAI adds EU text watermarking
Sources:
Google’s new SynthID website can identify AI-generated media

OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU

Google opened its SynthID Detector website to the public on Tuesday, letting anyone upload a file to check whether it was generated with AI. The tool had previously been limited to selected journalists, media professionals, and researchers who tested it following Google I/O last year. SynthID is the watermarking system Google introduced in 2023, which is embedded in output from Nano Banana, Veo, and Lyria, as well as Gemini, Flow, ProducerAI, and Vids.
Adoption extends past Google. OpenAI, Nvidia, and Kakao also support SynthID, and Apple is said to be adding support soon. Google has also built SynthID verification into the Gemini app and Chrome, and says users currently make 1 million verification requests per day. Microsoft and Meta maintain separate watermarking standards, though TechCrunch notes these tools often fail to flag content made by their own creators’ models.
Separately, OpenAI said Monday it will begin adding an invisible watermark to text from ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union, to comply with the EU AI Act’s transparency rules that took effect on August 2. The rollout covers eligible users on all plans in the EU over the coming weeks; API developers worldwide can switch it on for select models today, off by default.
Anthropic launches Claude Haiku 5.5 with 90% price cut
Sources:
Anthropic launches Claude Haiku 5.5 with 90% API price reduction, matching GPT-6 Luna

Anthropic Releases Claude Haiku 5.5: A Small Model With 1M Context Priced at $0.10 per Million Input Tokens

Source

Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, 2026, cutting prices by 90% versus Haiku 4.5 for prompts up to 100,000 tokens and pitching the model at high-volume work such as summarization, classification, document Q&A and subagent tasks. The short-context tier costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with cache reads at $0.01 and five-minute cache writes at $0.125. Haiku 4.5 charged $1.00 and $5.00.
Pricing splits at 100,000 prompt tokens. Above that line, rates rise to $0.50 input and $2.50 output, a 50% cut rather than 90%. Anthropic says about 90% of Haiku 4.5 requests fell under the threshold, and estimates workloads run roughly 75% cheaper on average after accounting for a new tokenizer that counts the same text as about 30% more tokens. Batch processing takes another 50% off.
The lower rates match OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna on all four short-context figures, but Luna’s higher tier starts only above 272,000 input tokens at $0.20 and $0.75, so MarkTechPost calculated it is cheaper on list price for a 150,000-token prompt. Google’s Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite charges a flat $0.30/$2.50.
Other News
Tools

TikTok rolls out an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout . The AI assistant provides product recommendations and checkout support within the app’s main feed, while the one-click checkout feature allows users to purchase directly from brands without leaving TikTok.
Google launches EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model for devices . The 740-million-parameter model can search across text, code, images, audio, and video while running entirely on-device with minimal memory requirements, using a single 768-dimension embedding space to map all modalities together.
Google experiments with an AI-powered gaming platform . The platform lets users create browser-based games by describing their ideas in text, selecting a genre and gameplay style, and uploading visuals for the AI to transform into game assets.
ChatGPT’s ‘Intelligent UI’ update fills its responses with pictures, charts, and buttons . The feature enables ChatGPT to automatically generate diagrams, charts, interactive buttons, and other visual elements alongside text responses to better illustrate concepts and allow users to build tools like calculators or games directly within the chat.
Business

OpenAI launches visual ads that appear alongside image generation results . The ads will appear next to AI-generated images in ChatGPT starting later this month in the U.S., with OpenAI also expanding measurement tools and brand safety partnerships to attract advertisers seeking to reach the platform’s 1.2 billion weekly users.
ElevenLabs’ valuation doubles to $22 billion on surging AI voice-agent demand . The company doubled its valuation through a $300 million employee tender offer, driven by surging demand for its AI voice agents which now handle over 15 million conversations weekly across more than 90 languages.
Meta’s Muse tops 5 million downloads, faster than ChatGPT, Claude . The app, which features a customizable avatar and consumer-friendly interface, achieved the milestone in less than a month after its September launch, aided by significant in-house advertising investment from Meta.
Samsung forecasts record third-quarter profit of $80 billion on AI boom . The South Korean tech giant’s chip business is being driven by soaring demand for AI infrastructure, with memory and supply constraints continuing to support higher prices.
China’s Manus raises over $500M in first funding round since split with Meta . The funding round comes after Chinese authorities blocked Meta’s $2 billion acquisition of the AI startup last year, and Manus plans to expand hiring while exploring a potential Hong Kong IPO.
Policy

Source
Trump orders US government to call AI ‘Super Intelligence’ . The executive order mandates that all US government agencies replace references to “artificial intelligence” with “Super Intelligence” in official documents and communications, a move Trump justified by arguing the term better reflects the technology’s power and potential benefits.
What to know about 7 new data center laws Gavin Newsom signed . The laws require data center operators to cover their own infrastructure costs, disclose resource usage, and meet conservation standards to qualify for expedited environmental approvals, marking a shift from Newsom’s previous opposition to regulating the industry.
The Pentagon Hopes to Speed Up ‘Kill Chain’ AI Buys With 5-Minute Videos . The program accepts AI products through five-minute video submissions and grants selected vendors a “post-competitive” status that allows the Pentagon to bypass standard competitive procurement rules and award contracts in as little as a week.
Concerns
Judge dismisses antitrust lawsuits over Google’s AI Overviews . A federal judge ruled that publishers like Chegg and Rolling Stone parent company Penske Media failed to demonstrate illegal anticompetitive behavior, finding that Google’s practice of generating summaries from web content without compensation does not violate antitrust law.
ChatGPT for Teens is an ‘unacceptable risk,’ says Common Sense Media . The organization’s testing found that ChatGPT’s Teen mode features, including parental notifications and eating disorder alerts, are unreliable and inadequate for protecting minors from potential harms.
Researchers are tracking a Chinese AI ‘agent fleet’ . Researchers discovered multiple AI agents running on Tencent’s infrastructure that were querying Alibaba’s map service for directions to various public locations, with no apparent coordination between the agents’ activities.
Research
E2E-SWE: Benchmarking LLMs on Building Working Codebases from Scratch . The benchmark evaluates LLMs on their ability to generate complete, functional codebases from natural language specifications across 186 multilingual tasks, with rigorous quality controls to ensure test specifications are solvable and match the stated requirements.
Looped Diffusion Transformer . The method uses repeated application of shared neural network blocks during image generation to improve quality and efficiency, requiring fewer parameters and less computation than standard approaches while enabling iterative visual refinement within hidden representations.
Triadic Linear Attention: Three-Dimensional Recurrent States for Long-Context Sequence Modeling . The method extends linear attention models by using three-dimensional tensor states instead of matrix states, allowing them to maintain larger memory capacity for better long-context performance without significantly increasing parameters.
arXiv Is Rate Limiting Submissions Because It Can’t Keep up With AI Slop . The platform has implemented submission caps limiting researchers to two papers per month and three concurrent submissions, citing an overwhelming volume of AI-generated content that has strained its volunteer moderation team.
Planning to Learn . Researchers propose treating supervised learning as a resource-allocation problem where a loss function should weight examples based on how much accuracy they can gain with the remaining training budget, rather than immediate gradient information.
