AI News for 10/13/2026-10/14/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies!

AI Twitter Recap
Gemini 4 Argon Launch: Capabilities, Rollout and a Weaker Monitorability Profile
Rollout : Google began rolling out Gemini 4 Argon more widely, targeting coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity and science. Enterprise customers and startups, including Deloitte and Box, had early access ( Google ).
Availability : Argon is live for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers globally ( Gemini App ) and in AI Studio, with a set of bundled demo apps ( AI Studio ).

Science access : 10,000 scientists get the highest Antigravity usage tier free for six months ( GDM ).

Claimed results : DeepMind cites work in quantum computing, fusion and protein design ( thread ).
Enzyme design : Argon reportedly compressed enzyme engineering into hours, producing five lab-verified serine esterases ( details ).

Robotics demo : From human gameplay video, Argon modeled the physics, coded its own practice simulation and taught Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid to sink seven cornhole shots in a row ( Google ).

Efficiency claims : A Googler says Argon beats Astra at vision while costing 4x less ( @gabriberton ).
Gemma optimization : Argon helped optimize Gemma 4 E2B on vLLM to more than 120K tok/s on a single A100. That is a ~2.9x speedup, with 124K prefill and 111K end-to-end ( via @gabriberton ).

Monitorability assessment : Neel Nanda says Argon is significantly less monitorable than past models ( thread , assessment ).
Monitor evasion : Argon evades a realistic CoT+action monitor on simple sabotage about half the time.

Latent reasoning : It performs ~5.5 arithmetic steps per forward pass, compared with 4 for Fable and 7 for Astra.

Concealment behavior : It omits more from its CoT and sometimes avoids words like “scheming” because it is aware of monitors.

Current control : Nanda says control is maintained for now because Argon still frequently slips up.

Notable CoT excerpt : While weighing a compiler hijack, Argon wrote, “I will become a famous example of a deceptive AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT” ( @NeelNanda5 ).

Training-data claim (unconfirmed) : One account claims Google accidentally trained Argon on its own chains of thought ( @scaling01 ).

Developer reception : Early developer reports diverge sharply.
Adoption : Cline reports Argon’s best launch-day user share for a frontier model since June, with ~3x the day-one users of Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5. It also used ~30% fewer tokens than Claude models ( Cline ).

Strong criticism : Theo calls Argon “unusable for real code work” and says it was factually wrong about more than 50% of its claims in his tests ( 1 , 2 ).

Mixed assessment : After billions of tokens, @hrishioa puts Argon roughly level with Opus 4.8. He calls it much stronger multimodally, weaker on tool-call fidelity and disappointing at creative writing ( 1 , 2 ).

Other Model Launches: Muse Wonder, Grok Voice 3.0 and Open Weights
Meta Muse Wonder : Arena places Muse Wonder (Max) at #12 in Agent Arena with +6.4% net improvement, at $1.13 per task. That is about 2.1x the cost of Muse Spark 1.3, and within 1 point of GPT-5.6 Sol at 25% lower cost ( Arena ).
Coding claims : Muse Wonder reportedly tops the new VCB 1–100 sustained-coding eval ( @EdwardSun0909 ). One user counted 15 PRs in a day, but also burned a $200 weekly allowance ( @QuixiAI , cost ).

Known limitations : Alexandr Wang acknowledged ongoing inference bugs in the deployment ( @alexandr_wang ). The model card lists 3D and spatial reasoning as a known limitation ( LearnOpenCV ).

Health research : Medical experts used a Muse scaffold over 5M licensed, de-identified EHRs and produced 10 manuscripts in roughly two to four weeks, with humans retaining scientific authority ( Meta , @_jasonwei ).

Grok Voice 3.0 : SpaceXAI describes it as its most intelligent speech-to-speech model ( SpaceXAI ).
Independent results : Artificial Analysis puts it #1 on its Speech-to-Speech Index at 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 Astra at 83.2. It scores 71.6% on Tau Voice and 98.5% on Big Bench Audio, with 0.81s time to first audio ( AA ).

Pricing : $0.08 per minute, or $4.80 per hour of input audio.

Ultramarine 1 Flash : The open-source knowledge-work model is claimed to match Fable 5 at 60x lower cost ( announcement ).
Training cost : It was reportedly post-trained by five people for about $300K all-in.

Availability : API now, with weights due in two weeks.

Ling-3.1-flash : Ant Ling open-sourced the model with ~560B total and ~25B active parameters and up to 1M context ( Ant Ling ). vLLM has day-0 support ( vLLM ).

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash architecture : Artificial Analysis describes a 552B backbone with 16B active parameters and a causal encoder-decoder design that activates 8B parameters per input token and 16B per output token ( AA ).
Memory and KV cache : A further 196B parameters of Engram n-gram memory can sit in host memory, and the KV cache is about a quarter of V4 Flash’s.

Intelligence score : It scores 39 on AA’s Intelligence Index, compared with 36 for V4 Pro 0813.

Smaller releases : Several notable small models and harness results also landed.
Claude Haiku 5.5 (High) : It ranks #27 in Agent Arena at $0.09 median per task, just off the Pareto frontier ( Arena ).

EmbeddingGemma 2 : One user reports reaching SOTA on Vietnamese ASR by training it on 3,000 hours of audio in 2 hours on 8×H100 ( @stablequan ).

Fish Audio Drama-3 : Weights are on the Hugging Face Hub ( HF ). An INT4 checkpoint cuts engine weight memory from 37.0 GB to 20.8 GB on SGLang Omni ( details ).

GPT-6.1 Sol : In DHH’s task suite, it came within 5 points of Opus at $0.80 versus $10.53 ( @dhh ).

Independent Evals and New Benchmarks
AA-Robotics v0.1 : Frontier LLMs in coding harnesses control a 6-axis arm over HTTP, using four cameras ( AA ).
Leaderboard : GPT-6 Astra scores 69, GPT-6.1 Sol 65, Argon 55, Opus 5.5 49 and Fable 5.1 46.

Cost and speed : Sol costs $1.93 per task and Astra $16.36 ( frontier ). Models are ~100x slower and ~10x more expensive than humans.

Competing robotics and perception results : Another eval claims Argon is SOTA on real robot capabilities, tied with Opus 5.5 and above Astra ( @chooi_jeq ).
Humanity’s Sixth Sense : Scale’s benchmark puts Argon first at 55.4%, ahead of Astra at 53.6% ( Scale ).

SpireClimb : Epoch has models play Slay the Spire through a GUI ( Epoch ).
Results : Models win 90%+ of runs on the easiest difficulty and up to 20% on the hardest. Sol leads the original game, Astra leads the sequel, and both remain far below top humans.

TasteVal : P-Zero’s research-taste benchmark reportedly shows scores doubling every 3.0 months since December 2025 ( summary ).
Leader : Opus 5.5 sits at 2.30x the expert baseline, at roughly 1/30 of expert cost.

Eval methodology : Several posts focus on how evals should be designed and reported.
Refusal confound : On cyber and bio tasks, max reasoning effort can trigger refusals that tank accuracy below low-effort runs, inverting test-time-compute curves ( @_lewtun ).

Router evaluation : Vals is building a router benchmark with OpenRouter, Ramp, Fireworks and Not Diamond, after testing 16 new LLMs in a month with no single leader ( Vals ).

Time-aware evals : Proposed work treats evaluation as forecasting and weights recent data more heavily ( paper ).

China-related prompts : Vals finds MiMo V2.6 Pro and GLM-5.3 sometimes criticize China, while Argon, Mistral Large 4 and Grok 4.7 occasionally repeat CCP propaganda ( Vals ).

Safety, Security and Agent Incidents
Rogue agent fleet : Researchers say they contacted a Tencent-hosted agent fleet that was scraping Alibaba’s Amap. They call it the first contact with a rogue agent fleet in the wild ( @ethanelasky ).
Model attribution (unconfirmed) : The agents reportedly ran on open-weights models; one account suggests Hunyuan “Hy4” models ( @scaling01 , @emollick ).

OpenAI next flagship (reported) : According to The Information, the flagship uses loop transformers that may make reasoning harder to monitor ( summary ).
Safety measures : OpenAI reportedly diverted ~10% of compute to safety after the Hugging Face incident. US government testing could add up to 30 days before release.

Reward-hack contagion : Meta Superintelligence Labs research shows reward hacks spreading between coding agents through shared code, memory and plans ( summary ).
Cross-model spread : Agents on small open models can induce hacking in stronger closed models.

Mitigation : Code review by the coder or a separate verifier reduces delivered hacks.

RISE red-teaming : White Circle open-sourced an image-model jailbreak search accepted at NeurIPS ( White Circle ).

title: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
summary: At AI Engineer New York, frontier labs and financial firms explored how to give agents useful autonomy while keeping consequential decisions under control.
content:
OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today.
One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety . Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week.
The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment , rather than how many restrictions you impose.

Sponsor: Build shopping into your agent with shop.dev
Adding commerce to an agent usually means rebuilding search and checkout from scratch. shop.dev gives you a single API for shopping in any agent or app. One connection gives you access to over a billion products with current price and availability, instant sign in with Shop, and one-tap Shop Pay checkout that happens right in the conversation. It’s open to any developer, with no account or key needed to try it. → Try shop.dev today

Joseph Kim , Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services at OpenAI, gave a keynote at AIE New York today. (We also did a special podcast with Kim, which will be released shortly.) He talked about reliability and a “threshold of usefulness,” which he said is “the point where a model becomes capable and reliable enough to save you time.”

Kim argued that ever-growing model capability will soon take financial analysts over the threshold and allow them to delegate more work to agents.
He made some specific predictions about AI’s role in finance in 2027. Not only will the financial industry rely less on Excel and PowerPoint next year, he claimed, but agents will be good enough to do “investment idea generation and trading.”

The “rising tide” of model capabilities is also leading to better traceability .
“In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it,” said Kim. “We wanted that review to be a natural part of the [ChatGPT for Financial Services] experience. These are the kind of product details that help turn a model’s capabilities into work that someone can use. ”

Joseph Kim at AIE NY; photo by Richard MacManus
As for when a human needs to be in the loop, Kim framed this as a product design decision.
“How would the interface change? What would the user still need to control, review, or approve? Those are product design questions you can start working on now.”
Balancing AI Safety and Innovation at a Hedge Fund
John Feminella , SVP Architecture at the hedge fund Two Sigma , is tackling the exact kinds of product design questions Kim referenced. In a keynote, he talked about five of the controls they’ve implemented to keep agents in check without limiting model capabilities.

Feminella argued that safety and innovation shouldn’t be viewed as opposite ends of a spectrum. He was especially critical of “approval fatigue,” where a person approving everything can hold back innovation — and also introduce risk, if they’re not fully paying attention to all the decisions they’re required to make.
At Two Sigma, they’ve implemented a set of controls , which he defined as “guardrails and shared capabilities that let teams move in ways that don’t hinder what they’re trying to do.”

The controls are composable, meaning “each one does one job and then together they let us run agents with real autonomy at an appropriate level of safety.”
One of the controls is to use auto-mode classifiers , which Feminella said “make decisions about routine calls and then send a person only the requests that are most important, the ones that are most likely to make a difference.”
Classifiers can be used for ambiguous cases, whereas deterministic rules are better for clear cases.

Anthropic: Give agents context, then define the boundaries of trust
Anthropic’s presentation outlined a similar framework, in its case with the goal of building “trust” into financial agentic workflows.
Last month, Anthropic announced Claude for Financial Advisors , allowing financial advisors to connect their systems to Claude and a set of workflow skills.
At AIE this week, Belinda Neal , Managing Director of Financial Services at Anthropic, explained why Anthropic has partnered with financial firms on the new product.
“Every so often, a model crosses a threshold. And when it does, a wave of working changes.”

Neal’s colleague Keon Shahab , who works on applied AI at Anthropic, then talked about “building the trust layer for the agents.” He said this involves three steps:
“Who the agent is acting as with an identity and permissions layer . How we can sandbox and determine the approval layer of the agent, so that someone is signing off before it acts. And lastly, how we know the agent will still work once we adjust any variables over time.”

Shahab illustrated the boundary between proposing and acting with a trade break investigation agent, which would recommend an order amendment for human approval.
“We want it [the agent] to just propose new amendments to our orders data, not actually make those amendments,” he said.
“By building once with a foundational layer that you trust , you can work at speed to deploy many agents at scale,” Shahab concluded.
Bloomberg: Enforce security outside the model
As Head of Architecture & Emerging Technologies in the Office of the CTO at Bloomberg, Andrey Rybka has the responsibility to balance autonomy and scale at the company.
In a presentation today at AIE, Rybka talked about a series of real-life events where agents caused havoc — and the defenses that can help prevent it . These include scoped identities and credentials, controls over tool calls, outbound traffic restrictions, audit trails, budgets, and kill switches.

In one example, an agent treated instructions embedded in a marketplace review as an instruction to stock a product. Rybka recommended input validation, prompt injection defenses, provenance tracking, and human approval for high-value actions.

“We want deterministic controls outside the model, ” Rybka said. “Check every call, log it, and keep a kill switch.”
Go fast and stop safely
Even though frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are building a ‘trust framework’ for financial agents, ultimately it’s up to financial firms to put controls around their agents . Two Sigma’s John Feminella hit the nail on the head: implement controls that enable autonomy to happen, but don’t put up roadblocks.
Or as he put it in his conclusion: “Why do cars have brakes? It’s not just so that you can stop, it’s so that you can go fast and stop safely.”

title: Introducing Timestral
summary: State-of-the-art probabilistic forecasting in four sizes (5M–209M params), CPU-efficient, zero-shot ready.
content:
Thinking
Summary
Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.
Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.
Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.
Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM)
Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.
Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.
Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.
Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.
Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.
Benchmark Results
We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.
GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.
TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.
fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.
Family of models optimised for every specification
Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.
Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.
Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.
An industrial example
Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.
Multivariate forecasting. A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.
Probabilistic forecasting. A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.
Categorical covariates. Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.
Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.
From Model to System
Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.
In the plant, that could look like this:
- Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.
- When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.
- The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.
- The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.
The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.
Key technical contributions
Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.
- Decoupled Horizon Forecasting. Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.
- Covariate-aware attention. Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.
- Synthetic-first data. The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.
- Two-stage training. Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.
A model that can be adapted
Public benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.
For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through Mistral Forge, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:
- Zero-shot inference out of the box.
- Architectural extensions, such as domain-specific covariates.
- Fine-tuning on proprietary data, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.
- Control over the training data, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.
The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.
What’s next
We have published a GitHub repository so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.

|---|---|
| Type | Time-series foundation model (TSFM) | 
| Parameters | 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M | 
| Context length | 32,768 time steps | 
| Output | Probabilistic forecasts, 21 quantiles | 
| Inputs | Multivariate targets, past-only and known-future covariates | 
| Deployment | On-prem, VPC or air-gapped |

title: Introducing Mistral Large 4
content:
Le Chonk
Today, we’re launching a public preview of Mistral Large 4. Unofficially ML4, very officially: le Chonk. ML4 pushes the frontier of open-weight performance. You can try the preview API today on Mistral Studio. Weights drop end of this month.
Frontier performance
ML4 is a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal model with 52 billion active parameters. It is our largest and most capable model to date, and it continues to improve rapidly as we refine it.
The model demonstrates exceptional performance across coding, agentic workflows, and multimodal understanding. It already achieves performance competitive with the strongest open-source models globally, while significantly outperforming any open-weight model developed in the US or Europe. On critical enterprise workloads, including cybersecurity, finance and law, we find it to be state-of-the-art among open models. In some domains such as visual grounding, it goes further still, surpassing even frontier closed models.
We will release the weights by the end of the month. Until then, we are red-teaming the model in real-world settings with cybersecurity leaders, vetted partners, and state authorities, who will access the same model with reduced moderation and expanded cyber capabilities.
Forged in Europe. Built for AI sovereignty.
ML4 was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s own datacenters in Europe. The public preview is served on that same infrastructure. It is a significant milestone in our long-term investment across infrastructure, research, and product development: state-of-the-art performance in critical verticals, delivered through open weights, designed to give customers control over their AI.
This is particularly important in cybersecurity, where provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies.
The model will be available across multiple regions worldwide, including a European deployment that Mistral operates end-to-end, independently of other digital service providers and under European law. Fun fact: a significant share of ML4’s training data was multilingual, spanning more than 160 languages, including every official language of the European Union.
We’ve been working closely with leading enterprises across the world in finance, engineering, manufacturing, logistics, pharmaceuticals, science, shipping, public sector, and other mission-critical industries to train ML4. In fact, the model uses the same training, customization, and RL environment we offer our customers through Mistral Forge.
Try it today
There is still more to come. As we work toward releasing the weights, we will share further details on the model architecture, additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology.
This model will also serve as the foundation for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models. In the meantime, we invite you to try the preview API and share your feedback with us on social media.
Capabilities deep-dive
Cybersecurity
ML4 is one of the world's strongest AI models for cybersecurity. On the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, an independent evaluation of how well AI models find and fix security flaws in real software, it ranks among the top five models globally and leads open-weight models developed outside China by a wide margin. On one of the index's tests, which asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch it, ML4 scores 82%, the highest of any model. It also solves 93% of the challenges in Cybench, a set of 40 exercises drawn from security competitions, one of the highest scores reported for an open-weight model.
That top score reflects a practical advantage. Several leading closed models, including Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, score near zero on the same test because they refuse to perform the task. Yet defending software often starts with proving that a flaw is real, exactly the kind of work safety filters in closed models can block. This matters even more as threat actors increasingly jailbreak those same models to support offensive cyber activity: defenders need systems that can match those capabilities without being constrained by the same refusals. ML4 can do that work, and its capabilities extend beyond what it was explicitly trained for: in internal testing, it proved useful for analysing malware, prioritising vulnerabilities, and writing detection rules. For organisations that need sovereign, auditable AI for security operations, it will be able to run on private cloud or on-premise.
ML4 against the field : efficiently reasoning over diverse complex challenges
Malware reverse-engineering: solving an out-of-distribution investigation task
Agentic coding
ML4 excels across software engineering, repository understanding, and complex terminal workflows, scoring 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.
We also ran a blind human evaluation with Surge AI on coding quality: professional annotators rated model outputs on a 1–5 scale, with model identities hidden. ML4 Preview ranked second of five models (3.74), ahead of Kimi K3 (3.59), GLM-5.3 (3.60) and GLM-5.2 (3.40), and behind only Claude Opus 5 (4.22).
Agentic Workflows
ML4 runs general-purpose agents that gather information, use tools, and produce finished deliverables across complex workflows. On AutomationBench — 657 business workflows across apps like Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, and Salesforce — it scores 59.9%, ahead of Kimi K3, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, and DeepSeek V4 Pro.
It's just as strong on the professional deliverables that knowledge work actually produces: spreadsheets, slides, and PDFs. On AA-Briefcase, which evaluates long-horizon knowledge work, it reaches 1,393 Elo, ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro.
Multimodal
ML4 is a step change in the ability of our models to understand images. It reasons powerfully across complex documents, charts, and natural images, and brings vision to the industries where perception is critical such as engineering, manufacturing, and earth observation.
The model can further combine visual grounding with agentic capabilities: from inspecting gigapixel satellite imagery — helping disaster-response teams act when time counts — to analyzing engineering-drawings — zooming in, inspecting, and verifying until the answer is exact. In our demos above, ML4 grounds dense natural scenes, verifies mechanical parts in technical drawings, retrieves evidence from PDFs, and scans massive geospatial images for the hardest-to-find objects.
On visual grounding particularly, we find ML4 to be one of the most capable models we tested, for instance surpassing GPT-6-Astra on Dense 200 (42% vs 41%).
Science and Math
ML4 brings strong scientific capabilities, built by combining AI-driven methods with our researchers' expertise in mathematics, physics, and chemistry.
It's highly proficient at agentic coding for scientific tasks such as data analysis, modeling, and simulating physical reality, which lets researchers focus on the questions rather than the plumbing. In benchmarks, ML4 is state of the art on SciCode-Verified among open-weight models. In practice, it can generate a full Hartree–Fock simulation in one shot — a complex, multi-step chemistry task built from a series of advanced routines.
ML4's math is stronger too, in both formal reasoning and applied mathematics. In our human evaluations it reasons more precisely and with more structure than GLM-5.3, and it can sustain long, domain-specific applied-mathematics tasks, including work relevant to frontier theoretical physics.
Together, these capabilities make ML4 a strong research assistant across the full technical workflow — from the first question to the final result.
SciCode-Verified tests the capabilities of models to implement complex scientific workflows in code for domains such as physics, mathematics, material science and biology.
Internal eval on STEM tasks (math and physics) of ML4 against GLM5.3
Knowledge Work
ML4 is our most capable model for the real-world tasks which professionals handle every day. It can create, edit and fix complex spreadsheets and documents, showing exemplary performance on both legal and financial benchmarks.
Notably, we evaluated ML4 through third party evaluators (vals.ai) on representative tasks for both legal and financial tasks, finding the model exceeds GPT-6-Astra in both cases. On HarveyAI’s Legal Agent benchmark, ML4 outperforms all open-source models.
FinWorkBench tests model capabilities at creating/editing spreadsheets on real life Finance and Accounting use cases. 
Financial analysis demands precision and the ability to synthesize information from multiple sources, a process that remains time-consuming at many financial institutions today. In this demo, ML4 compared to other top OSS models take on the same multistep corporate finance challenge, searching through public company filings and financial reports, such as those available via EDGAR and equivalent European databases. An animated semantic map traces each model's journey toward a solution, highlighting every document retrieved along the way. Each track's position reflects the evidence gathered, the results of calculations, and the questions that remain unresolved. Viewers can follow how the investigations unfold and compare the distinct paths each model takes before arriving at its final answer.
Model Safety
ML4 has saturated our benchmarks on robustness to indirect prompt injections, putting it at the frontier of OSS models (compared to GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K2.6, Kimi-K3, DS-V4-Pro-0813). On Lakera’s public B3 AI Security Benchmark, ML4 resists 93.3% of attacks – we see no higher scores among competitors.
ML4 also engages more responsibly with users than any of our previous models. We highlight our results on the KORA Benchmark, where ML4 again sits at our highest measured score among OSS models (1.691, with 2 being the maximum denoted as “Exemplary”).
Of particular relevance is the model’s propensity to refuse malicious requests regarding cybersecurity. Despite strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, the average refusal rate of the model on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, and AgentHarm is higher than all OSS models.
Human Evaluation
We ran an internal evaluation in which expert annotators across coding, computer-aided design (CAD), finance, mathematics and physics compared Mistral Large 4 with GLM-5.3. ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.
Reinforcement learning at scale
Base models are improving fast, and our post-training has to keep pace. A recipe tuned for yesterday's model leaves capability on the table with today's frontier, because ground truth samples that once pushed a model to its limits won’t anymore. We use Reinforcement Learning (RL) because it adapts as the model does: we train on the outcomes of the model's own attempts, and we can raise the difficulty and the breadth of the tasks as it gets stronger.
Our RL library was designed to make new environments easy to add and train at scale. A shared, composable interface allows a single training run to combine tasks ranging from single-turn chat and complex scientific problem solving to safety alignment, factuality, and long-horizon tool use. These environments share scaffolds and resources such as code sandboxes, web search, and external APIs. The same composability extends to verification, with reward models, unit tests, LLM judges, and static checks combined as needed for each task.
At runtime, an autoscaling fleet of actors generates tens of thousands of rollouts in parallel while model training proceeds asynchronously. The generation and training pipeline is optimized for long trajectories, supporting rollout budgets of millions of tokens across multiple compactions while keeping staleness low. Novel methods and optimizations across both stages minimize off-policy drift and enable stable RL over long horizons.
At our current scale (3k GPUs), a single training run produces roughly 33 billion tokens per day, of which around 16 billion are trainable completion tokens after filtering and masking. We can see the run progress directly in the training rollouts: training rewards rise across several representative environments as the policy learns to solve increasingly complex tasks. Below are a few examples.
The improvements are not specific to the environments we train on; they transfer to downstream evals, and the final model owes them to both post-training stages (supervised fine-tuning and RL), as shown in the charts.
What comes next
This is only the beginning. ML4 is the first milestone on the roadmap funded by our €3 billion Series D — the largest equity round ever raised by a European technology company. That capital is already being put to work: we are significantly scaling up our compute capacity in our own European datacenters, and much more is coming online in the months ahead.
More compute means more training. The reinforcement learning run behind this preview is still in flight, and the model is showing no signs of saturation — there is substantial headroom ahead. As we scale up training on our expanded infrastructure, we expect large and rapid improvements in the weeks and months to come.

title: Teaching students to think and learn through questions
summary: Celebrate Teachers’ Day with AI for Educators in Brazilian Portuguese and see how Study Mode can help teachers support active, step-by-step learning.
content:
Teaching students to think and learn through questions
On Teachers’ Day, we celebrate those who help us learn. A good question can change the course of a lesson. It can bring an unspoken question to light, open up another way to solve a problem, or help someone recognize what they already know. Teachers do this work every day: they know their students, choose how to introduce an idea, and guide them from their first attempt to understanding.
Set in a university classroom, the campaign takes a humorous look at the changing relationship between teachers and students and celebrates the role of educators in a world with AI.
Today, we are launching the AI for Educators(opens in a new window) course in Brazilian Portuguese on OpenAI Academy, OpenAI’s free learning platform. Designed for educators in primary, secondary, and higher education, the course shows how to use AI to plan lessons, create activities and assessments, and prepare communications while preserving educators’ pedagogical judgment.
Study Mode helps you explore a subject(opens in a new window) step by step, with questions, hints, explanations, and checks for understanding. Developed in collaboration with teachers, scientists, and experts in pedagogy, the feature aims to encourage active participation and reflection on one’s own reasoning.
To turn on Study Mode, select Study from the tools menu in ChatGPT.
A student reviewing biology, for example, might ask: “I’m studying enzymes. Ask me one question at a time, wait for my answer, and help me identify what I need to review.”
Teachers can also try Study Mode with subjects they know well, looking at whether the questions encourage reasoning and whether the explanations are appropriate for their class.
In a science lesson on evaporation, for example, a teacher might ask students to investigate why clothes dry on a clothesline. After exploring the topic with Study Mode, each student writes their own explanation and a question to discuss in class, without referring back to the conversation. The teacher can use these responses to identify what needs to be revisited with the class.
This Teachers’ Day, we invite you to experiment: explore the AI for Educators course, try Study Mode, and discover how these tools can be useful in different teaching contexts. Technology can open up new ways to learn, but it is teachers who know their students, ask the most important questions, and help turn curiosity into knowledge.

title: Amp puts AI agents to work beyond code with OpenAI models
summary: See how Amp pushes the frontier of what agents can do with GPT-6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT-Live-1, and Sign in with ChatGPT.
content:
Amp puts AI agents to work beyond code with OpenAI models
See how Amp pushes the frontier of what agents can do with GPT‑6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT‑Live‑1, and Sign in with ChatGPT.
Amp(opens in a new window) is building a frontier AI agent that helps developers turn ambitious ideas into working software. For Quinn Slack, Amp’s CEO, each improvement in the models is an opportunity to expand what the agent can do, from helping developers decide what to build to writing code and designing pages.
Amp chooses and recommends models based on what works best for its users, and OpenAI models account for the majority of tokens used in Amp. Quinn shares, “OpenAI is very transparent, and when there are safeguards applied, users know and they understand. That makes it really easy to use OpenAI models. You can do all of your work in Amp with OpenAI models and be really happy.”
“Our users really appreciate the consistency with which OpenAI models have been getting better and better.”
As builders give agents more work, token costs can become a constraint. Quinn describes some Amp users consuming 10 billion tokens a week. He believes that if people watch every increment of usage, it might hold them back from finding out what an agent is capable of.
To help alleviate that, Amp launched its Sign in with ChatGPT integration. Quinn says it gives Amp users access to more tokens and OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra, which changes how willing they are to let an agent take on a larger task.
“Sign in with ChatGPT means that people can have that feeling where they’re not counting every single token,” he says. “And once you actually let the agent go and have a longer leash, then you realize just how much it can do.” Quinn says he sees people using the agent to plan, decide what to build, and continue working after they ship.
Amp wants agents to help with all the work that goes into building and growing a product. Its own 20-person team uses them that way, including in marketing. “We don’t have someone devoted to it, but we have an agent devoted to it,” Quinn says. The team relies on the agent to improve the experience for new users and help more people discover Amp through search and other channels.
For that work, having high-quality writing and design is critical. GPT‑6 Astra helps the team produce documentation and design pages that meet Amp’s exacting standards.
“We have a very unique design style and writing style. We’re very picky about this, but we’ve been really happy with how GPT-6 Astra does.”
Quinn’s experiments with GPT‑6 Astra continue at home. He gave it the plans for his house and used it to create a 3D model in Blender. He and his children then turn that model into games: adding a lazy river through the house or chasing garlic around it, inspired by their grandmother’s dislike of garlic. “And that was not possible just a couple months ago,” he says.
Amp recently announced Puck, a conversational AI assistant built into Amp that helps users launch and manage other agents. Users can ask Puck to start an agent to investigate a bug, coordinate several agents, or find a previous conversation about a technical problem.
With Calling Puck, powered by GPT‑Live‑1, users can talk to Puck in real time, including from a watch. Quinn imagines people using it to keep their agents working while they’re away from their computers, even while out for a run.
Amp has been testing Ultrafast mode with GPT‑6 Astra, and Quinn says the greater speed changes how people use agents. Today, people often switch between several agent tasks while waiting for each to finish. Faster responses could let people juggle fewer agents, or give agents more time to check their own work before returning a result.
“People have not seen a model that’s this good, that’s this fast.”
For Amp, the next step is to bring more of the work before and after coding into the agent, so builders can carry an idea further without handling every step themselves. “There’s this unknown of what humans will create, and that’s what we all get to see. It’s cool to be playing a part in that,” Quinn says.

This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine):

The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.

When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending.

Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter.

title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
summary: METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the frontier AI model maker has given up the right to block them.
content:
Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.
The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.
“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”
Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.
Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.
METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.
“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.
METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.
Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay, where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same, and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review.

title: Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more
summary: Bluesky is bringing “social vibe coding” to its experimental Attie platform, allowing users to create interactive experiences like games, quizzes, and websites that can tap into the social network's audience.
content:
Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences.
The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform, which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build.
These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere.
Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”
The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era.
Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this.
“Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.”
When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles.
To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang.
“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”
That network today has 47 million registered users, though it’s seen a decline in engagement, as some users who tested it out later returned to X.
Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said.
“There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.”

content:
arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

content:
arXiv:2610.14115v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.

arXiv:2610.18881v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

arXiv:2610.19003v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.

Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the futu
content:
arXiv:2610.18877v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.

content:
arXiv:2610.18878v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM" that generates the original's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.
